1 would now like to discuss briefly the Conservative mortgage interest tax credit proposal. As with the issue of Petro-Canada, this government seems determined to push ahead with something which just does not make sense to anybody. This year we will be asked to approve over half a billion dollars for a program which will eventually cost the treasury over $2 billion. Why? It will not make housing any more accessible. In fact, increases in interest rates have more than offset what little benefits home owners are going to get this year.
The American experience shows that eventually benefits get built into the cost of housing and that banks and development companies are the only ones who really benefit from the scheme. This new scheme will not stimulate construction. It does not benefit renters and those who have already paid off their mortgages. The mortgage interest scheme is just a political gimmick for which the Canadian taxpayers will end up paying. If the government is really serious about helping the average Canadian acquire decent, affordable housing, let it use CMHC. We have the instrument to stop land speculation, to initiate social and co-operative housing projects on a massive scale to bring down the cost of housing. Members of our party believe that mortgage interest rates should be reduced. They should be brought down to 8 per cent for families earning $25,000 or less per year. In conclusion, Canada is facing a number of crises: world energy shortages affect our lifestyle, inflation and economic uncertainty undermine our labour, environmental pollution threatens our health. We have reached a point in human history where man has finally become capable of total selfdestruction. After millions of years of survival we stand on the brink of extinction. These are sobering thoughts, but if hon. members have been listening, they will know that 1 am not alone in this belief. Concerned thinkers and scientists throughout the world are raising their concerns. A new approach to development and economics is required. We cannot afford to continue with the outdated concepts of growth which we have been promoting for the past 200 years. We must have development which makes sense for people, not for profits! In some small way this was understood many years ago in Saskatchewan. The people realized that co-operation would make life better for everyone, so they co-operated. It is not perfect, but people understand that collective action can be taken to solve problems.
The Address-Mr. G. Richardson
The people of Saskatchewan woke up to the fact that the free market system was exploiting them, that the free market system was not so free, that the free market system works well for bosses and owners but does not do very much for the little guy, the average worker and farmer in the country. We in Saskatchewan fought back. We started to take control of our destiny. Saskatchewan Crown corporations are working in the interests of the province. Any profits that are produced are turned over to the provincial treasury to fund social programs and further economic development. Saskatchewan people own a large chunk of their province through Crown investments. Saskatchewan people own and operate these companies. Saskatchewan Government Insurance will never leave Saskatchewan as Sun Life left Quebec. The people of Saskatchewan own their own insurance company; they direct its activities.
Canadians can learn much from the Saskatchewan experience. They can learn to take control over their lives, to direct their own future and to co-operate. Also Canadians will learn that governments can plan ahead, that governments can make life easier and our rewards fuller. Today Canadians are seeking a greater voice in the development of this country. They have good reason to doubt the ability of the federal government to look after their best interests. While Liberals and Conservatives continue to promote their outdated economic theories, our party will demonstrate that we have alternatives, that we can plan an economy which will reduce unemployment, decrease inflation and provide proper health and social services for all Canadians. We will not allow industries to pollute our air, water or land. We will ensure that the environment is cleaned up and protected for future generations. We are not pessimists, we are optimists. It is not a dog-eat-dog world as far as we are concerned. We believe in co-operation and sharing. We are our brother's keeper. We have faith in the human race. We have faith in people's ability to work together to solve their common problems. We have faith in the future. We have faith in the vast human and social potential which can make this land and this planet a peaceful place in which to live, free from starvation and want, exploitation and greed.
Perhaps the best way to sum up would be to paraphrase the first leader of our movement, J. S. Woodsworth, who said, "What we desire for ourselves ... we demand for all".

speechtext:
I thank the people of Humboldt-Lake Centre for electing me. I assure them I will do my best on their behalf. Indeed it is an honour to be the first representative from the new riding of Humboldt-Lake Centre, the heart of Saskatchewan. The riding contains over 12,000 square miles of inhabited farmland, four potash mines, seven Indian reservations and some of the finest people in Canada. It is situated mainly in the park belt area and contains some of the best farmland in Canada, particularly in the northeast corner. It is strictly a rural riding being made up of the rural areas of the former seats of Saskatoon-Humboldt, Regina-Lake Centre and Regina East. Part of it is the original Lake Centre seat in which Mr. Diefenbaker was first elected to Parliament in 1940.
Times change, populations decrease and Saskatchewan lost four seats in a redistribution. Lake Centre was put in with Moose Jaw and Mr. Diefenbaker had to move to Prince Albert, a seat which he held until his death in August. The title "Lake Centre" has been retained as part of the constituency name in honour of our former prime minister, the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker.
At this time I should like to pay a brief tribute to Mr. Diefenbaker. He was never afraid of what men said. He always believed in what he did. One of his favourite quotes was that he was never always right and sometimes on the wrong side, but he was never on the side of wrong. He had the ability to bounce back, even when he lost the leadership at the 1967 convention. He went back to his hotel, shaved, put on a white shirt and said the equivalent of: let us go out and save Canada for Canadians. Mr. Diefenbaker made the Conservative party a progressive party. I believe it was his motion which added the description "Progressive" to the name Conservative. Whether this is true or not, it is a fact that he turned the party of the privileged into a party of the people, a party which believes in the worth of the individual and the values of private enterprise. He will be remembered as one of the greatest Canadians of all time.
This is a new government. We are facing the dawning of a new era. Unfortunately we are beginning in very difficult times. At the moment the annual budget deficit is approximately $11 billion. Our foreign exchange account is in a deficit position by several more billion. The United States appears to be going into recession, and the possibility exists of being dragged along with them. However, I firmly believe that if we fulfil our election promises, much can be done to alleviate the situation and put us on the right track to balance budgets and bring about a thriving economy.
Coming as I do from an agricultural riding, my first concerns naturally are for the welfare of agriculture and farmers. But let us face it, Mr. Speaker, when agriculture prospers, the rest of the nation does likewise. Even though Parliament was not in session, this government has been very active. One of our prime concerns, in the west at least, was to get grain moving and to put some cash in the farmers' pockets. We have

set ourselves the target of increasing our grain export capacity by 50 per cent by 1985 to meet the Canadian Wheat Board's projected increase in marketing possibilities by that time. When we became the government in May, we faced the fact that in the crop year just ending the railways had handled one million tonnes less grain than in the previous year. Because of the previous government's failure to move sufficient grain in the 1978-79 crop year, we are going to have to increase our handling by 20 per cent this year, and by 10 per cent each year thereafter until 1985, if we are to meet our target and commitment.
In this matter, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski) stated this morning that we are ahead of last year. We are taking action, and the wheels are already in motion. Some 5,000 rehabilitated boxcars will be coming onstream this year. In addition to these, there will be 2,000 Canadian Wheat Board tankers coming into service. Thus the grain handling fleet will be increased by 7,000 cars in one year. The Murta commission, headed by the hon. member for Lisgar, has made many useful recommendations which will speed up the turnaround times of grain cars. The Minister of Transport appointed the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) to meet officials of the elevator companies, and the lines which will be kept and upgraded have probably been selected.
An agreement on the development of Prince Rupert has been signed. Improvements to the over-all system are being rapidly undertaken. The appointment of Dr. Hugh Horner as a grain controller will speed up matters. Because of possible bad weather, strikes and various disasters, such as the one that has just hit the CNR bridge in Vancouver, it is never safe to predict success. However, prospects are bright and we may well achieve our target of a 20 per cent increase in grain shipments this crop year.
A couple of days ago, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael) told of the virtues and achievements of the previous government. Let us face it, Mr. Speaker, in a democracy all governments have some virtues and achievements. However, I maintain that we as a government have achieved in five months as much as they did in five years. The hon. member for St. Boniface mentioned the revised quota system. It was a good quota system too because it brought millions of dollars to the pockets of farmers in western Canada.
The idea for that quota revision was mine. In 1969, at a meeting of Mr. Stanfield with grain producers in Regina, 1 broached the idea of a quota revision, but I was told by Mr. Hamilton that we were not in power at that time, which I accepted. We were not in power and we could not do anything about it. I passed that suggestion along through the Federation of Agriculture to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board at that time. He saw the value of the idea and immediately instituted a quota revision committee. The basis of that quota revision was a new quota system which resulted in millions of dollars ending up in the pockets of the farmers of western Canada over the years.

Although it was my idea, they took the credit, but that is fine because we all benefited. If you transferred that idea from here to there, Mr. Speaker, you would see that we have achieved more in five months than the previous government has in five years.
There are also other matters of deep concern to me. With regard to energy self-sufficiency, it is very important that we stop being dependent on foreign oil. The Speech from the Throne stressed this point.
We promised a once in a lifetime exemption from the capital gains tax on the sale of a farm. This is a measure that is very important so far as farmers are concerned. It is also a measure which should be extended to the sale of small businesses. We hope that in time this will be possible.
During the campaign we also promised to inject some common sense into the previous government's mad rush to convert to the metric system. The appointment of an overview committee to discover how far the change-over has gone and make sensible recommendations is a step in the right direction.
I hope to have time to return to this matter a little later.
The Speech from the Throne promised to implement our mortgage interest and tax deductibility scheme. Regardless of what the interest rates may be, those who are buying homes will still be helped by the scheme.
Last year, 20 per cent of the construction industry was unemployed and there were some 70 per cent unsold housing units in Canada. This scheme will help get those housing units off the market, will encourage new housing starts, will get construction workers back to work, and help an industry which is 100 per cent Canadian, using 95 per cent Canadian material in its work. What better way is there to help Canadians than by putting them to work building in Canada?
The matter of ever increasing interest rates is of deep concern to this government. The Progressive Conservative Party has always been considered the party of lower interest rates. The mandate given the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to look into all aspects of the situation and bring in recommendations should help toward finding a solution.
Small business is the backbone of this country. It is being badly hurt by ever increasing interest rates. It is the intention of this government to do something about rectifying this situation.
Returning to our promise of a once in a lifetime exemption from capital gains tax on the sale of a farm, I hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) will be able to implement this measure in his first budget. It is very important that he do so. So far as the farmer is concerned, his property is his pension plan. Because of his ever increasing productivity, he is one of the greatest inflation fighters we have. Why should he be made to pay for inflation that he did not cause?
The present roll-over features in the tax laws are not satisfactory. Under these regulations, a farm can only be transferred to a son or a daughter. A farmer cannot transfer his farm to his sister free of capital gains tax, even though the
The Address-Mr. G. Richardson sister might have worked with him on that farm all her life. If he cash rents, he is no longer considered to be a farmer. He would have to sell his land to his son or daughter at the full market value as determined by the most recent sale of land in that vicinity. He would have to pay the full capital gains tax and his son or daughter would have to pay the full going price of land in that area.
It may be only a few years from now that a would-be farmer will not be able to afford to buy land from an heir who wishes to sell, because the heir will have to have so much money in order to pay his capital gains tax and have something left for himself that he would have to charge an outrageous price for the land. The only purchaser available then would be either a large corporation of government, for instance the Saskatchewan government land bank. In Saskatchewan now-I was given these figures the other day-there are some 914,000 acres of land already under the land bank and some 54,000 acres due to be purchased this year. We have to make it possible for the would-be farmers to buy land, and this once in a lifetime exemption from capital gains tax on the sale of a farm would seem to me to be the answer.
Land ownership by farmers on family farms has been the basis of progressive, productive agriculture throughout generations past. Continuation of our present course will result in takeovers by other than farmers-large corporations, governments and the like. Placing our farms under state ownership or corporation management lowers productivity and puts our future food supply in jeopardy.
Removal of this tax by allowing the farmer his once in a lifetime exemption on the sale of a farm would allow him to sell to anyone at a lower figure because there is no tax to pay. It would allow a family member to buy at a lower Figure and be able to pay for it. It would keep ownership in the hands of the farm operator. It would enable him to produce for less, and at the same time productivity of the farms would keep going up, with society as a whole being the beneficiary.
As I said before, I would like to see this regulation extended to small businesses. During the campaign we promised to eliminate the capital gains tax from the sale of public Canadian stocks and bonds. Some 70 per cent of the small businesses in Manitoba, for instance, including farms, are not listed on the stock exchange. The elimination of this tax for them would help equally as much as it would the farmer, and we hope this will take place in the future.
Personally I have always questioned the value of a capital gains tax in a country like Canada, a country that is perpetually short of development money. It does not make sense to me to transfer potential Canadian investment capital to the nonproductive sector by using a capital gains tax, then going abroad to borrow more capital at higher interest rates, further upsetting the foreign exchange and balance of payments accounts. I am told that less than 1 per cent of this tax goes into revenue, the rest of it being used up in administration. We are paying dearly for that 1 per cent in lost potential Canadian

The Address-Mr. G. Richardson
investment capital. Far too much potential Canadian investment capital has gone abroad because investors could get a better deal, a better tax break and a better margin of profit. It is the intention of this government to reverse this trend. It is the purpose of this government to encourage Canadians to invest at home.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, with regard to this mad rush to metric that was instituted by the previous government-

speechtext: Metric madness.

speechtext:
It is metric madness, you are right. Seventy per cent of the people in my constituency would put a moratorium on this metric changeover right now.
Personally I am not against changing to something better. I am for those changes that will give us an advantage in the marketplace or make daily life easier and reduce the price of product to the consumer. I believe that the units of measure we use should be the most practical ones; the ones with which it is easier to operate, the ones that will cost the economy the least, the ones that it will be to our advantage to adopt, whether these units be imperial units, metric units or some of each. This mad, indiscriminate rush to metric change-over has achieved the opposite result.
Perhaps I should elaborate on some of the foolish changes in measurement the previous government forced us into. As a farmer I have had units of measurement forced on me that were not asked for, were not needed and are not practical. I refer specifically to the bushel and the tonne.
A few years ago our international grain trade was conducted in tonnes, the farmers were using bushels and everybody was happy, if not with the price at least with the unit of measurement. Today the average farmer does not know where he is at. He has been forced to deal in tonnes at the farm level and a tonne is just something that cannot be visualized. The bushel is a unit of volume as well as of weight. The tonne is a unit of weight but its volume cannot be estimated. A farmer can look at a field of grain and estimate the bushels on it within a very small margin of error. There is no way he can estimate tonnes or kilos. He can look at a bin and tell you immediately how many bushels he has in that bin; he can multiply the bushels by the price per bushel and give you his net worth just like that. He can go and talk to his banker and get his loan. He cannot do this in tonnes without carrying around a bunch of tables and a pocket calculator. When seeding in bushels we knew what we were sowing, and when harvesting we knew what we were reaping. Quotas in kilos or tonnes mean nothing to us whereas quotas in bushels do.
A few years ago, and even up to the present, it did not matter to the Russian or the Chinese buyer, whoever bought our grain, whether the farmer delivered the grain to the elevator in bushels or tonnes. That buyer was receiving the grain in tonnes in any event. Why was this impractical tonne measurement forced on us at the farm level? As it is now, the railways are still paid for hauling in hundredweights and car

capacities are listed in pounds. Where is progress made as a result of taking away our bushel and switching to metric?
I received a letter the other day from a small storekeeper in the village of Bruno, Saskatchewan. That storekeeper is being forced to buy metric scales at a cost of several thousand dollars with no trade-in value on his standard scales. These small merchants, the backbone of small communities, are finding it hard to make a go of it. In a small town of 400 or 500 people, and I come from one, how many thousands of dollars worth of groceries do these storekeepers have to sell just to pay for the scales? These small storekeepers cannot afford this kind of thing.
Referring now to lumber, if all our mills were switched to metric what would we use to repair all the standard size buildings in North America? A metric piece of plywood is three inches shorter and an inch and a half narrower. Sheer necessity would force us to produce in both standard and metric. The size of lumber yards would have to be increased to handle the different units. It would be necessary to have two production lines of equipment instead of one, and what that would do to the price of lumber I can guess. This would create problems and extra work for the mill men trying to fill orders for windows, doors, cabinets, lumber, etc. If followed, the actions of the previous government would force us to buy two sheets of metric plywood to repair that hole in our standard wall where the purchase of one standard size piece would have been sufficient. What a mess our livingrooms will be with cracks, joints, spaces and everything else all over the place! One standard size panel would have filled the need nicely.
To my way of thinking it would have been better to allow the person who wanted to use metric to buy a standard sheet and let him cut the three inches off the end and the inch and a half off the side. In this way we would only need one production line, not two, and in this way we would only create one set of problems, not two. The point I want to make is that to date common sense has not been used in this matter of metric change-over.
The manner in which metric change-over was handled by the previous government was an insult to the intelligence of the Canadian people, and a costly insult at that. Industry knows when changeover will be beneficial to it. Farmers, storekeepers, consumers in general know what they want and what is good for them. When they want change they will ask for it, and the time for changing should be of their choosing. That is democracy, Mr. Speaker. In addition to that, when 70 per cent of our trade is with the United States any process of changeover should be in tandem with them; that is, we should change as they do.
I should like to commend the Minister of State for Small Business and Industry (Mr. Huntington) for appointing an over-view committee to study the progress of metric conversion. I am sure this committee will bring in some common sense recommendations that will let us either retain or convert to the unit that best serves our purpose, be that an imperial unit, a metric unit, or some unit yet to be devised.
October 18, 1979

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am sure this Thirty-first Parliament will be one of the most productive, progressive and at the same time conservative Parliaments we have ever had.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in the throne speech debate. I extend my congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, on being re-elected as Speaker of this House. It is an historical event because I believe it is the first time a member of the opposition has been elected to serve as Speaker in this House. It reflects the confidence which both sides of this House have in your abilities, and I am sure that they will be challenged in this minority Parliament, making your duties that much more onerous. I hope that your ability to judge wisely and your fairness will continue. Those of us from northern Ontario feel it a great honour that one of our own should be elected Speaker of the House. I know that hon. members who served on the back bench on the government side in the last Parliament look forward with great anticipation to the much wider latitude you have always provided to members of the opposition, especially during the daily question period.
I would also like to extend congratulations to Senator Grosart on being elected as Speaker of the other place. He has been a member of long standing in the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association and I sure that this will stand him in good stead in his new appointment. Of course, as Speaker in the Senate he will also be the honorary president of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association.
I also want to extend congratulations to the former speaker, Senator Lapointe, on the character and the ability with which she served in this high office for several years. She did so with great style, grace and charm, and she has been an outstanding ambassador for Canada when she travelled abroad, whether replacing the Speaker of this House or acting in her own role as Speaker of the Senate.
I congratulate the hon. members for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) on their respective replies to the Speech from the Throne. I believe that they performed in the best traditions of this House, and hopefully have started what will be very good and worth-while parliamentary careers.
I extend my appreciation to the people of Algoma who last May 22 made what I believe was a very wise decision. I appreciated their support and encouragement on election day. Algoma riding takes in parts of Sudbury and Manitoulin districts as well as Algoma District on the north shore of Lake Huron, and it carries on up along the Lake Superior shore.
There were two significant changes which took place in the constituency this year. Some 15 per cent to 20 per cent of Sault Ste Marie, that area north of the second line and west of Allen's Side Road, was brought into the Algoma riding which resulted in some 11,000 electors being added to the constituency. I look forward to serving those constituents from that important city.
The Address-Mr. Foster
Likewise, since the last federal election the town of Elliot Lake has grown dramatically. It is one of the fastest growing towns in the country. In fact, if this Parliament should last as long as the Thirtieth Parliament, though I do not believe that it will, it will probably be a city by the time of dissolution.
With the last redistribution, there is almost a 50 per cent increase in the number of electors in my constituency, which spreads out along a rural area of some 400 miles from just south of Wawa in the northwest to Nairn Centre in the east, and includes Manitoulin Island, the largest island in fresh water in the world. I believe that it is one of the most challenging and interesting constituencies in the country and that it has the best electors. Of course, the challenge is the same to each and every member in this House, and that is to represent our electors in the House of Commons and to serve them in the constituency. That is what I plan to do as we begin this Thirty-first Parliament.
The election of 1979 is a long way behind us now. We have had the longest break between the election call and the opening of Parliament in the last 44 years. I think that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) indicated that this time was necessary. It is worthwhile to look at some of the things which have happened during this period while the House was not sitting. Certainly there have been some very harmful and very negative occurrences in my constituency.
Specifically, I refer to the decision made in early July to locate the new uranium refinery for the province of Ontario in Port Hope, just on the doorstep of metropolitan Toronto. This was a terrible blow to the economy, planning and hopes of all the municipalities along the north shore of Lake Huron. We believed that this Crown corporation would be located at Blind River on the north shore of Lake Huron. This move represents the loss of some $100 million in capital investment and 235 new jobs in an area which has one of the highest employment rates of any area in the province.
I believe that it is the policy of this government to locate the refining of uranium and other mineral resources from northern Ontario on the doorstep of metropolitan Toronto. With such a policy it will be a long time before we in the north achieve those economic and social goals which we look for. As if to add insult to injury, we learned last week via the news media that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) and Eldorado Nuclear had announced that the nuclear waste of that refinery will be disposed of in Algoma.
It seems to me as though this government has no conscience, no heart and no soul. How could any reasonable person or government suggest that the resources will be mined and milled in the north, then refined in southern Ontario, which means that that area receives the benefit of the capital invested and the jobs available, and then after refining the uranium the nuclear waste will be sent back to the north? It is totally unacceptable. I hope that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will reverse this decision and locate the new uranium refinery in the north where it should have been in the first place.

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Foster
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) this summer decided to cancel the Canada Works program. This will have a disastrous effect on many of the communities in the Algoma-Manitoulin area which has depended on this program for some 400 to 500 seasonal jobs each year. This program has meant the spending of $1.5 million to $2 million on municipal and community projects, mainly through the municipal councils and Indian bands. There are approximately 4,000 to 5,000 status Indians living in the Algoma-Manitoulin area on 12 different Indian reserves. This program, which had created employment and benefited many of the communities, will now be replaced by unemployment insurance or welfare payments. Such a move was a cruel blow and most unfortunate for our community. A few weeks ago we had a seminar on employment programs for young people. We found that this Canada Works program, which we normally think of in terms of seasonal employment during the winter and spring months, was in fact utilized by young people to the extent of 45 per cent.
The new government came to power promising a great deal of economic activity and a chance for the private sector. On reading the Toronto Star yesterday, a headline suggested that the government was planning to impose a 23-cent excise tax on gasoline; this on top of a $4 increase in the price of a barrel of crude oil. If this report is accurate, then surely we are in for very, very hard economic times.
Yesterday in the House, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) told hon. members that he wanted to get that oil price increase behind him and get on with the building of the economy. I can see why he wants to get on with the building of the economy and get the oil price increase behind him, but if that oil price increase is to be 30 cents or 40 cents, as has been rumoured in press reports, we will not be getting on with the building of the economy very rapidly this year. It seems to me that if we are facing a 40-cent increase in gasoline prices, this will have a disastrous effect on the economy. An impact like that on the economy would be the equivalent of striking a weakened man with a baseball bat. As a result, the consumer price index will probably get pushed up 4 per cent to 5 per cent, giving us double digit inflation and a weakening economy.
The premier of Ontario has talked about the loss of 20,000 jobs in the province. His emissary, Mr. Miller, has come to Ottawa today to try to persuade the government not to move in such a drastic and harmful way. Mr. Blakeney, Premier of Saskatchewan, along with premiers from the Atlantic provinces, has expressed concern and denounced the move. All the sweetness and light of federal-provincial co-operation that we were told about during the election campaign seems to have gone down the drain over the last 24 hours.
I want to turn now to the report delivered by the task force on Monday. It seems to me that the proposals for the national petroleum corporation, Petro-Canada, require a review before being adopted by this government. In my opinion, the most

devastating effect would be that of the government having to pay off approximately $1.5 billion and then having to turn around and give the shares away. Surely if we are talking about cutting back government expenditures, putting an item of $1.5 billion in the supplementary estimates next spring will require a lot of fund raising from one source or the other. I do not know if this report that about 23 cents excise tax will be loaded on gasoline prices is true or not. Perhaps that is the way the Minister of Finance will raise the $1.5 billion that would have to be paid off if the task force report is implemented.
Instinctively I feel there will be harmful effects if the government pursue this action. If we are in a tight Financial situation, why deliberately assume an obligation of that size just to give something away? If we were to follow the procedure outlined by the task force report and at the same time the minister were to impose a 23-cent excise tax on each gallon of gasoline, we would have a situation whereby the Prime Minister by his own handiwork would be handing out a few shares of Petro-Canada worth maybe $100 and there would be an imposition of $150 in excise tax in order to get the money back. In a situation like that, no one gains. And, the real hooker is that we continue to pay the excise tax year after year, whereas the $100 worth of Petro-Canada shares, as proposed in the task force report, would be a one-time thing.
This report proposes an agency to take on all the risky ventures. All the things Petro-Canada is doing would be put into a company called Petro-Canada Exploration, which would be given away to the Canadian people. The risky things, such as the high Arctic exploration and the activities offshore on the east coast where this year the drilling of one well cost $25 million, would be assumed by this agency. Each year this agency would have to come back to Parliament to get approval for money required for exploration, for research into and development of tar sands technology, and so on.
At the present time Petro-Canada, because of its activities in the conventional western basin, is generating revenues in the order of $350 million in cash flow this year. That Figure is projected to be $550 million next year from its investments in Pacific Petroleums, Atlantic Richfield and others. I am told it is generating enough revenue that it will not be necessary to approach Parliament for two or three years for exploration funds. If we adopt that task force report, we have to pay off the $1.5 billion and then give it away. The agency taking the place of Petro-Canada would be coming to Parliament each year for funds for exploration and development.
There are other disadvantages as well. For example, there is a penalty involved. If the federal government were to pay off all the preferred shares owed to the banks in the Petro-Canada Corporation, a $20 million penalty is required to be paid by it. As one reads through the report, it will be seen they have tried deliberately to break up the activities of the national petroleum corporation-such as Panarctic, the Polar Gas project, and the Arctic pilot program-into projects that make money and ones that do not. We find that these shares are broken down. Obviously, it is a very difficult exercise, and I would hope that the government would not jump into that
October 18, 1979

proposal lightly. In my opinion, there are some natural disadvantages, the main ones being the financial cost to the government and the lack of direction which will result because it is paying most of its concern to generating profits and to paying a dividend to shareholders.
I think PetroCan has shown that it can give impetus and encouragement to the private sector and involve little investors and small exploration companies in its activities, but at the same time it is always working in co-operation with the private sector. It does no individual exploration. Those items should be carefully considered by the government before moving to implement the report. In my opinion it would be harmful and would not allow the national petroleum corporation to continue with what it is achieving now.
When members of this House went to work in 1975 to establish this corporation, I do not believe many of us thought that it would achieve as much as it has in the first three or four years it has been in place. I am surprised that the government is persisting with its plan to dismantle Petro-Canada.
A Gallup poll that was taken shows that 48 per cent of the people polled want Petro-Canada maintained, while 22 per cent said they did not. A more recent Gallup poll I believe has been more supportive than that. It is only three or four years since the bill establishing this corporation was passed, yet we have a major Canadian company owned by the Government of Canada and therefore by all Canadians. This company is big enough to stand up to the big foreign-owned multinational corporations that it deals with every day. It also has an influence on the whole industry. Petro-Canada is the sixth largest petroleum producer in Canada today. It is in the same league as the multinationals, and many of the other state owned oil companies which most countries have around the world.
Petro-Canada has taken an active role in exploration in the Arctic Islands. In 1978, 16 of the 26 wells drilled in the most remote frontier areas had PetroCan participation. PetroCan has the largest land possession in the eastcoast offshore, giving Canadians a real chance at the tremendous activity and development expected to take place there. In the Hybernia well, where there was an oil discovery this summer, the only Canadian player in the game was PetroCan. It has a 25 per cent involvement.
Let us look at state trading which was a role of PetroCan and is not in limbo. Before this government was elected, Canada was in a position through PetroCan to make a deal with Venezuela and Mexico for some 100,000 barrels a day so that we would not be dependent on the multinationals such as Imperial which last year proposed to cut back some 25,000 barrels a day of oil. That was during the Iranian revolution.
In the negotiations signed by the former minister of energy, mines and resources, Mr. Gillespie, we had a $5 billion agreement whereby we would be buying their non-renewable resources and they would be buying our manufactured goods, items of high technology like the Candu reactor. That agree-
The Address-Mr. Foster
ment has been in limbo since the election. I understand the French have moved in and have taken the position for 100,000 barrels which would have been ours, and prospects of deliveries by Pemex, the Mexican national petroleum corporation, have been sharply reduced.
These negotiations with Venezuela and Mexico are now in limbo. No activity is taking place. In a recent delegation that went to Mexico, there was only one PetroCan official as an observer. We see as well that the Japanese have taken our place in line. They are not negotiating for 100,000 barrels a day but for 200,000 to 300,000 barrels a day. They are talking about a pipeline across Mexico and a port on the west coast.
Countries like Mexico and Venezuela have indicated they want to trade on a state basis in the future. They find it incomprehensible that this government is considering dismantling our national petroleum corporation. When the Prime Minister was in Japan in June, he indicated that our net petroleum requirements of offshore crude oil by 1985 would go from 200,000 today to 600,000 barrels a day. He promised to cut it from 660,000 to 600,000 barrels a day. It has more recently been suggested that by 1990 it might be 800,000 barrels a day.
When Sheik Yamani, the minister of energy for Saudi Arabia, was here, he suggested the real crunch would take place by 1985. At this time a year ago, there was some surplus in crude oil supplies in the world, but by 1985 the demand will far exceed the supplies. Of course, the real crunch will come then.
State to state negotiations will become more and more important in the future. The government has indicated it will leave state to state trading with the proposed agency or Crown corporation, but they have left it in limbo. Instead of hiking their way down to Mexico or Venezuela to complete negotiations, they have been in limbo since then.
PetroCan has taken an active role in the Syncrude project and other projects in the west such as the tar sands, the Lloydminster heavy oils project and the Cold Lake project of Esso Resources. This is fitting. It is certainly our most important ace in the hole. There is no certainty that future oil supplies will be discovered in the western basin, the east coast offshore or in the high Arctic. We know the tar sands are there. It is a case of finding capital investment and of overcoming environmental concerns to bring it onstream. PetroCan has been and should continue to be active in that.
Negotiations with Lloydminster and Esso Resources have been in limbo for the past six months. In the last three or four years of its existence, PetroCan has been a real catapult in exploration in the Arctic. If we look at the Whitefish discovery in the Arctic Islands last spring where three trillion feet of gas was discovered, we see that the initiative for that Arctic Island exploration group came from PetroCan. However, it did not invest all the money; there was something like an 18 per cent investment. Much of the rest came from multinational corporations which launched on a five-year program that will cost $80 million. It has already discovered significant reserves of natural gas.

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Foster
In my opinion, we will not get that kind of initiative with the type of company proposed in the task force report on Petro-Canada. We will lose that. It will be a self-perpetuating management more concerned about paying dividends to its shareholders, which it should be, than taking risks and bringing onstream four or five years earlier the oil and natural gas resources that we need.
The same is true of the Sable Island discovery last summer. When PetroCan first went in there all other exploration had ceased in that area. They spent between $40 million and $50 million on exploration and made a really important discovery there. Although they had been ridiculed by the industry, the industry followed along and went in and now they are only a minority shareholder. If that well of last summer is proven, there will be adequate gas for almost three times the needs of the maritime provinces. It will change the whole energy pattern in those provinces.
In the Newfoundland-Labrador shelf, nine of the 11 wells drilled off Newfoundland this summer have had PetroCan investment, including the Hybernia well where oil was discovered. PetroCan was the only Canadian participant in that project. PetroCan s initiative on the east coast has stimulated a great deal of exploration and development there.
It is interesting to note that the Premier of Newfoundland, Mr. Peckford, is one of the most lively and enthusiastic of PetroCan's supporters. It is a pity the Prime Minister does not listen to his counterpart in Newfoundland.
To put that kind of activity that is taking place on the east coast offshore into perspective, some $600 million has been spent during the last 12 years on exploration and development there. This year it will be $300 million. That shows the kind of enthusiastic activity that is taking place this year while a few years ago activity was very low. If oil is discovered there in quantities large enough to be produced, it will be in the right place because it is on the east coast that we import most of our oil.
PetroCan has been intimately involved in the Arctic pilot project, which is a liquefied natural gas proposal. It is designed to use tankers and a gasification scow to liquefy natural gas in the Arctic Islands and ship it by tanker to east coast ports. The capital investment involved is much smaller than would be required for a pipeline. It gives us flexibility in the movement of natural gas in liquefied form to all the east coast ports.
Even more important is the ship technology which would be involved. There would be important spin-offs for delivering minerals and ores from the Arctic Islands. We are building up significant gas reserves in the Arctic Islands and this is the most favourable project at this stage, certainly from a financial point of view, because, as I say, not so much capital is needed as would be needed for the building of a pipeline. Using two ice-breaker tankers under that scheme we could process some 250 million cubic feet of gas per day, the equivalent of 40,000 barrels of oil a day, for the east coast. With the acquisition of Pacific Petroleums, PetroCan was

placed in a much more favourable revenue position and I hope that before the government destroys or dismantles the national petroleum company it will listen to members of Parliament on this side, to members on its own back benches, to the provincial premiers and, most of all, to the wishes of the Canadian people. They want the corporation to remain in force to ensure our supplies of petroleum in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate. As usual at the beginning of a new Parliament, I would like to extend customary congratulations first to the Governor General who admirably discharges his duties and shows a thorough knowledge of Canada. I am also pleased to see you back in the chair, Mr. Speaker, because you have discharged your duties with much dignity and fairness during the last Parliament. I would also like to congratulate sincerely the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. There is no doubt that they are destined to a fine career and I heartily wish them the best.
I cannot refrain from mentioning the changes which have occurred in the House; thus, the former leader of the opposition (Mr. Clark) has become Prime Minister. We wish him the best of luck in carrying out that difficult task given to him by the electors. I am convinced that the former prime minister (Mr. Trudeau) who is now Leader of the Official Opposition will lead his troops with as much ability as in the past.
I also extend my good wishes to the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) for his skill in speaking French. I should not forget either the leader of my party, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy) who brings on the federal scene his invaluable experience.
My best wishes are directed to all new hon. members who make their debut; I wish them as much success as possible. The hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) stated yesterday that he had been welcomed by all hon. members, except those of the Social Credit Party. I dare hope that he did not mean what he said; so, my best wishes to him, and 1 wanted to say "Tungasugit" to him, which means "welcome" in his language.
Mr. Speaker, as you can see my colleagues and I are getting closer to power, but what I fear most on this side of the House is to be asked questions by my Liberal colleagues. I hope they will recognize that we share the floor of the House with the Progressive Conservatives, but we do not necessarily share their policies.
It is customary at the beginning of the first speech to praise the beauties of one's constituency, which I hasten to do. I have had the honour of representing the constituency of Rimouski for seven years. This year, the area of Temiscouata was added to the area of Rimouski to form the new constituency of Rimouski, which will be called Rimouski-Temiscouata eventually, as I put forward a bill to that effect. I should like to thank
October 18, 1979

all my electors who enabled me to sail across the "Red Sea", and I repeat what 1 have always said: Once elected an hon. member is at the service of the population. Whatever the political barriers may be, above all else human beings must be taken care of. I can assure my fellow citizens of the riding of Rimouski that 1 shall be available and devoted to them.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne is the first opportunity the government has given us of evaluating the situation in our country and the solutions it intends to bring as the elected government. The government party made many promises during the last election campaign. To what extent it will live up to those promises remains a mystery. But one thing is sure, and that is that Canadians want a drastic change in the direction given the management of our country. They want a sound and stable economy, favourable to the young. I rejoice when I hear the government state that it will stress co-operation with the provinces. I was one of those who, in the past, opposed systematically the prevailing atmosphere of confrontation. And so, we were offered a plateful of good intentions that had been so reduced that the hungriest could not eat their fill. Here is the problem, Mr. Speaker. We have never really had a truly economic policy. Preceding governments merely implemented measures without too much concern about their repercussions, going ahead somewhat blindly.
When we draw a picture of the future, we cannot help doing it in the darkest colours. Our young people are not sure that jobs will be available for them when they leave school. The rate of unemployment remains at a level which is unacceptable to a society worthy of the name. The rate of unemployment in Quebec is 9 per cent. In my region of eastern Quebec, the level is intolerable. Early last summer, it reached 22 per cent. It is a fact that this level was reduced somewhat during the summer months, but because of seasonal factors only. Faced with such a situation, talents are wasted, lives are jeopardized, and our young people are powerless to deal with an uncertain future.
While on this subject, I should like to remind the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) that a new policy affecting the distribution of control regions for the computation of unemployment insurance entitlement came into force in November, 1978. It was claimed that this policy would take the economic realities of the various regions into account. This is certainly not the case in my own riding. It is made up of two separate areas, one which is attached to the Lower St. Lawrence-Gaspe region, and the other to the Quebec City region where the criteria are clearly less advantageous, while the rate of unemployment is about the same in both areas of my riding. The rate of unemployment in the Lower St. Lawrence-Gaspe region is about the same as in the Quebec City region.
Mr. Speaker, unemployment is a real problem, we must not hide the truth and be afraid to say so, especially when it is as high as it is today. Not only does unemployment completely upset the economy by generating a slow paralysis of all
The Address-Mr. Allard
activities, but it jeopardizes the capitalist system itself. Either the system will find a way to make it disappear or unemployment will some day make what is left of the system disappear.
The real solution to unemployment and inflation is not to create jobs at all cost but to change our present social system and allow all citizens, no matter what their status, to enjoy our country's wealth, even if they have no job, since as consumers they are integral parts of our Canadian economy. The solution we have been advocating for many years is to bring the retirement age from 65 down to 60 or less, according to the rising rate of unemployment. Then we would strike the necessary balance in the equation between industrialization and consumption. During the first six months of this year, Mr. Speaker, the unemployment rate in the Lower St. Lawrence area has shown such variations as 17.9, 22.8, 23.7, 19.8 and 17.9 per cent.
In the Quebec City area, it reached 9.4 per cent, 10.7 per cent, 11 per cent, 9.1 per cent and 7.3 per cent. It is therefore obvious that these rates have nothing in common. This is why I ask the minister to review the boundaries of this area so that the region of Grand Portage may be included in the Lower St. Lawrence-Gaspe area to determine benefit entitlements. [English]
Mr. Speaker, may I also take this opportunity to review quickly the state of our economy. Unemployment is a great concern, but the unemployed are not the only ones left out by our economic system. Farmers are not particularly privileged in our system. They are faced with much red tape and many regulations. Quota allocations are constantly reviewed, so that farmers cannot plan on a long-term basis.
People 65 and over also have to fight to obtain minimum living support. My friends in the government used to listen when I debated this question during the last Parliament, but now that they are on this side of the House I wonder if they will be receptive.
[ Translation]
In the last few years, I have suggested an optional retirement pension plan at 60 which could be established progressively. It would ensure better distribution of government funds. In this way, the jobs liberated by these people would go to the unemployed and we could save considerable amounts in unemployment insurance and reduce the financial burden of the old age security system. As I was saying, my colleagues in the government were very receptive to this idea. Will they still be as receptive now that they are on the other side of the House?
What about the poverty which still exists in spite of all the social legislation passed by Parliament? Last year, the Senate estimated that 43 per cent of the people living on their own were below the poverty level. These are mostly older people, which supports the suggestion that I made earlier. There are also 22 per cent of Canadian families in this situation. Poverty,
358

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Allard
inflation, unemployment, those are all important challenges which threaten all Canadians. In view of all this, the Speech from the Throne does not contain much hope. It refers to a few isolated measures, but does not mention any real medium or long-term economic policy. The government has adopted an attitude of laissez-faire in the hope that the situation will improve by itself. The previous administrations gave the impression that they left everything to luck. When Canadians protested against incredible inflation rates, a commission was created. Five were established during the last few Parliaments to study, control or review prices and especially wages, and they were then abolished. I was quite happy when the present government abolished the latest of these Liberal inventions.
Concrete problems require concrete solutions. Since 1971, the cost of living has increased by 90 per cent. The dollar has gone down 20 per cent compared with the American dollar. And since we are talking about statistics, I shall give a few more. In 1978, the government had a deficit of $12 billion, or 20 times more than in 1974. The deficit will be even higher this year. My colleague from St. John's West, who is now Minister of Finance, was the first to be shocked by this situation in past years. If he wants to take strict action, now is the time to do it. Our debt continues to increase at an alarming rate.
Last year, we had accumulated a $40.5 billion debt and we paid over $5 billion in interest, $240 per capita. Over the last five years, bankruptcies more than doubled in Canada, and rising interest rates are pushing credit out of reach, which implies that investments will slow down and people intending to buy a home will prefer to wait until conditions get better, rather than paying rates of up to 1414 per cent.
Such is the situation confronting members elected to this new Parliament. We should concentrate on this and see to it that this government discharges its duties as soon as possible. The people today expect and are entitled to a minimum of sincerity and honesty from politicians. Last year, while corporations increased their profits by 25 per cent, our unemployed, our farmers, our old aged pensioners and all those asking for a fairer share of this country's riches felt no improvement.
I have given many statistics, enough maybe to make us forget the human consequences of our economic difficulties. Our party always favoured throughout its history a human approach to our society's various problems. We believe in giving first place to the human being. We have consistently proposed reforms to that end. We believe among other things that each citizen must enjoy a minimum of physical and social security. We therefore propose a system of guaranteed annual income. The first duty of any government is to guarantee that every individual and family has sufficient income to be reasonably well off.
Mr. Speaker, economical justice also means fairer distribution of development across the nation. If certain economic areas continue to be favoured at the expense of others, national

unity will be left without much support. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest that the government consider an economic recovery plan for remote regions, for example by implementing a transport policy beneficial to these regions so that they can also have their rightful place under the sun.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath) no doubt remembers when it was announced that allowable cod catches in the Gulf of St. Lawrence would be increased. In this regard, also, the people of the Gaspe peninsula are at a loss since 10 per cent of these additional quotas will be for vessels of 100 feet or more which are harboured in the gulf or elsewhere. The problem lies in the fact that fishermen from the Gaspe peninsula do not have large vessels and those vessels of 100 feet or more will come mostly from other areas. I would therefore ask the minister to reconsider his decision which discriminates against the Gaspe peninsula fishermen.
Mr. Speaker, as a duly elected political group in this House, we could, according to the rules of procedures, introduce a motion condemning the government, but since the government must have the opportunity to prove its good will, we will allow it to do so. That is why we voted the way we did last Monday on the motion put by the Leader of the Opposition, but we can always change our mind.

I sincerely hope that this session will be the occasion to draw all the dynamic forces of this country together. Canada is at the crossroads of her history. Many decisions are facing us, and they will not always be easy to take. Quebeckers are about to make a decision which will affect all of us, whatever the result. I hope that the government will show an attitude of change and co-operation with all provinces so that Canada may be a better land for our children.

First I would like to assure hon. members that as I make my remarks this afternoon I am completely free of conflict of interest. I say that because I was involved in the oil industry for 20 years. However, prior to my nomination as Conservative candidate for Calgary South, I divested myself completely of any interests in the oil industry. I hold no management position nor do I serve on any board of directors or any committee.
The subject which I wish to address to the House this afternoon is on the issue of Petro-Canada. In my opinion, it is unfortunate that the issue of Petro-Canada has been blown so much out of proportion by the media and by the opposition parties in this House, particularly in relation to future energy supplies for Canada. It seems to me that this controversy is
October 18, 1979

relatively unimportant compared to the more serious problems facing Canada today.
Just to put the issue of Petro-Canada in some perspective, let me say that the company had total assets of $3.3 billion as of December 31, 1978. At the rate at which we are importing crude oil into Canada, this amount is equal to the cost of six months' crude oil imports. In other words, in the short period of six months, Canadians have consumed crude oil equal to the assets of Petro-Canada. It is in light of this that I believe the matter of Petro-Canada has assumed far greater proportions than is warranted.
At the same time, it is important for Canadians to understand what Petro-Canada is as it stands today and what can be achieved by individual Canadians owning shares of that company. The opposition would have Canadians believe that the solution to the energy crisis lies in the choice between Exxon and Petro-Canada; that is, multinational ownership or state ownership.
In the last five years, a revolution has been going on in western Canada and in the oil industry generally. The number of companies owned by Canadians has been increasing at a significant rate. Today, there are over 700 companies finding and developing new oil and gas reserves. Most of these companies are Canadian owned. They are responsible for 75 per cent of the wells drilled in western Canada, and there are numerous stories involving Canadians who have become important factors in the oil and gas picture.
I am absolutely confident that the oil industry will find the oil and gas reserves we need for self-sufficiency, given the economic opportunity to do so.
There is no question that the people of Canada distrust the giant oil companies. I think this distrust is largely unfounded. Consumers, not only in Canada but in all industrial nations, have been the great beneficiaries of cheap oil supplies for many years. Surely it would be foolish to cast aside the benefits that Canada receives from the large multinational oil companies simply on the basis that they are very large, with huge budgets, and that they are the object of the popular suspicion that bigness brings. The multinational oil companies have had great success in finding oil, some of it in hostile environments. They have enormous reservoirs of extra expertise. It would be irresponsible to do anything but encourage them to search as aggressively as they possibly can in Canada.
I simply cannot understand how economic nationalists can say that the repatriation of the Canadian oil industry from the United States investor is in the best interests of Canadians. In the next ten years, Canada will need about $200 billion just to develop our energy resources. Canada cannot provide this money by itself; it needs foreign investment. But how can we possibly encourage foreign investors when they do not know if their investment is going to be nationalized? Certainly much of the oil is foreign controlled. Why is that? It is because the former Liberal government would not offer Canadians the incentive to invest in their own country.

speechtext:
The private sector, the Government of Canada, and the provincial governments must all be deeply committed to the performance of their roles which are, respectively, petroleum operations and the design of a public policy framework. Both public and private participants must contribute to the accomplishment of clearly desirable national objectives.
Let me return for a moment to the fall of 1973 and 1974. Because of the Middle East war there were fears of shortages of oil in Canada. It was largely on the strength of the realization that Canada could not rely on cheap foreign oil to supply our needs that the former Liberal government came to the conclusion that one of the vehicles to be used to improve Canada's security of supply would be a national oil comany. Ostensibly this was the main reason for the establishment of Petro-Canada. But the Liberal government was so concerned about extending government control to the private sector that it lost sight of the basic energy needs of the Canadian people. Since that time, Petro-Canada has been put forward not only as a national saviour in terms of security of supply but also as a "window on the industry" and as a necessity for state to state oil trading.
The original mandate of Petro-Canada was to explore for and develop new sources of oil and gas supply for the country in areas where the conventional producers were not prepared to gamble. But what did Petro-Canada do? It purchased Atlantic Richfield and Pacific Petroleums. Did these acquisitions add any new reserves of oil and gas to our Canadian inventory? No, not a drop. Virtually all these reserves were acquired by the purchase of Atlantic Richfield and Pacific Petroleums. These reserves were in the ground in Canada and were completely secure for the people of Canada. Atlantic Richfield and Pacific Petroleums could not export any reserves without federal government approval.
It is interesting to note also that in 1977 Petro-Canada had 151 million barrels of oil reserves. At the end of 1978, these reserves had declined to 143 million barrels, a net loss of 8 million barrels for the year.
Security of supply is achieved when new oil reserves are found or new technology is developed to enhance production

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Thomson
from existing reserves. New oil is found by long and diligent work and expertise. It is not found by acquisitions, by buying companies that already have it. In fact, much of the expertise acquired through the acquisition of Atlantic Richfield and Pacific Petroleums has since left Petro-Canada.
Pacific Petroleums was a well-managed, successful and aggressive company. It was doing all the things any oil company could be expected to do and it was not costing Canadians one cent. It was finding new reserves; it was helping to create security of supply. Let us also remember that the purchase of the various assets Petro-Canada now owns did not contribute to the creation of any new jobs which otherwise would not have been created by the acquired companies if they had been left on their own.
It is simply untrue that the acquisition of Pacific Petroleums will provide Petro-Canada with a cash flow from existing oil and gas production to help finance the search for new oil and gas supplies in the development of heavy oil fields. The cash flow from Pacific Petroleums will not even service the interest on the debt incurred to purchase the company.
Also I should like to point out that it is not true there is any need for a government-owned oil company to make investments which otherwise would not be made. The recent example of exploration success in the Beaufort Sea demonstrates that if the ground rules with respect to taxes and pricing are satisfactory, shareholder owned companies will become involved of their own accord in all the risk taking which Canada needs in this or any other industry.
In his motion of non-confidence, the leader of the New Democratic Party sought to secure for Petro-Canada a monopoly on all imports of oil into Canada at a time when our supply is uncertain and insecure and when the international oil companies still have much of the foreign oil under their control through contracts. Surely common sense would suggest that a course opposite to that of the New Democrats should be undertaken. We should seek as many channels through which essential oil can flow as possible, not restrict the means to import oil. We should take full advantage of the worldwide oil network provided by the big companies, the so-called Seven Sisters, and if there are any useful ways of adding to this, we should do that as well.
One of the criticisms over the proposed sale of Petro-Canada to Canadians is that it is necessary for the federal government to keep a window on the industry through ownership of a large oil company. This is sheer nonsense. I should like to point out that in the blue book of estimates for 1979-1980 the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is staffed with no less than 12,180 man-years of bureaucracy to keep a window on the industry at a cost of $200 million. In addition, the Petroleum Corporations Monitoring Act provides volumes of information to the government. The oil industry is monitored from every standpoint and is likely the most highly regulated industry in our country. The necessity of having a window on the industry is nonsense.

There has been much discussion about the advisability of having a Crown owned corporation to effect purchases of foreign oil from foreign government-owned companies, and if necessary Petro-Canada should be utilized for this purpose. A better method would be to negotiate an international trade agreement with the particular country which is to supply oil, and then have commercial agreements negotiated within the terms of that treaty by private companies in Canada that would use the oil. This would serve the dual purpose of giving the Canadian government better control over the acquisition of foreign oil, while leaving commercial terms to private industry. Our government recognizes that it has a responsibility to fulfil with respect to state to state oil supplies. However, it is not necessary for Petro-Canada to carry out this function. Our government intends to do everything possible to ensure adequate supplies of a vital commodity which we will have to import in increasing volumes during the 1980s.
Where does Petro-Canada stand today? Let us remember that the original purchase of Petro-Canada was made by placing an additional tax burden on Canadians. The taxpayers of this country put up $800 million in equity to fund Petro-Canada, which is the equivalent of over $300 for every man, woman and child in Canada. This money came out of the pockets of Canadians in taxes which they otherwise would not have had to pay. The taxpayer also has ultimate liability for $2.5 billion worth of debt Petro-Canada has incurred. The financial structure of Petro-Canada as it now exists is overburdened with debt in relation to equity. Its debt is three times its equity, compared to a ratio in the private sector of the oil industry of about one-third debt to equity. In other words, Petro-Canada has nine times the amount of debt in relation to the equity of the private sector.
In 1978 it earned $13.3 million on an investment of $3.3 billion. This rate of return is less than half of 1 per cent and is an appalling mismanagement of taxpayers' money. We must remember that the government is borrowing money at the rate of 10 per cent, while PetroCan makes less than one half of 1 per cent. Shareholders of any public company would not tolerate such a disgraceful profit performance from its board of directors and its management. In the first six months of 1979 Petro-Canada lost $7.6 million. The reason for this loss is that the company cannot generate sufficient income to pay for the interest costs on the debt incurred to purchase Pacific Petroleums.
Petro-Canada is attempting to carry out the impossible, the dual roles of a commercial company and an agent of federal government policy. It is an impossible position of conflicting interest. The conflict between political goals of a government and the goals of a commercial corporation is at the root of what is wrong with Petro-Canada. When a Crown corporation such as Petro-Canada is charged with the frequently conflicting responsibility of serving broad national objectives and showing an appropriate profit from the use of resources under its control, such conflicts place the senior technical personnel and officers in an inherent state of uncertainty. They must make difficult decisions as to which objectives should take
October 18, 1979

precedence, frequently with incomplete knowledge of the urgency of national priorities. I say that without intending to malign the management of Petro-Canada.
Resources are not efficiently used when the objectives of a company are not clearly stated. There is an old saying in business: "If you don't know where you are going, any road will get you there". Those who control the company have an uncertain accountability. Profits may be attributed to good business judgment, while losses may be attributed to the fulfilling of national objectives. Who is to know? Certainly not the Canadian public with the set-up we have at the moment. Crown corporations are never free from political interference. It has been amply demonstrated by numerous Crown corporations that in every instance of direct government involvement in business they have problems running commercial operations without special breaks and subsidies. What our government is seeking to do is to maximize the benefit from the use of taxpayers' dollars. Maximum benefit results when government limits its role to public interest activities which are not commercial.
It is imperative that individual Canadians understand our serious oil deficiency. If the individual Canadian is directly involved in Canada's energy future, he will have a better opportunity to understand the energy problem. Certainly government must be responsible for public interest activities designed to assure secure supplies of energy for all Canadians. However, government need not engage in activities which are more effectively and efficiently served directly by its citizens, whether citizens invest as individuals or are organized in business.
I support the recommendation by the task force that Petro-Canada, as it presently exists, be divided into two parts, one which will be a private sector company and one which will continue to be an agent of the government and have direct responsibilities for activities which appropriately lie with the government.
The task force has recommended, and 1 agree, that the public sector responsibility would be transferred to a new government agency with the following functions: the negotiation of any necessary state to state oil supply contracts; the promotion of increased frontier exploration; and the promotion of oil sands and heavy oil research and development.
The private sector company, a new Petro-Canada, must be given a firm mandate to conduct its affairs on the basis of commercial viability. It must be absolutely clear that Petro-Canada will not be an instrument for the achievement of the government's public policy objectives.
I support the concept that individual citizens will be better served by having their energy investment reside directly with the private sector company. In this way shareholders will have the democratic right to influence policy through the decisions of the annual meeting or through the board of directors.
The new Petro-Canada as described by the task force can be the largest Canadian-owned petroleum company and its board
The Address-Mr. Thomson
of directors must be free to develop corporate policies which will permit the achievement of commercial objectives in a responsible way. Because Petro-Canada will have to compete, it will constantly be accountable to its shareholders, the citizens of Canada, for the efficient use of its resources and the resulting profits. Mismanagement will quickly become evident.
Canadian citizens, through their direct participation in Canada's new petroleum company, will be involved in the rewards and the responsibilities of ownership, and at the same time the new company will have the responsibility of encouraging citizen involvement and will recognize its direct accountability to its citizen shareholders.
The task force has again recommended that only eligible Canadian individuals should be entitled to receive shares in Petro-Canada, and only eligible Canadians should be permitted to acquire shares in the after market. I completely agree with this. A new Petro-Canada is assured of being a wholly Canadian-owned company. Individual investors should be limited to 1 per cent of the common shares outstanding. Every citizen in this country would be eligible to receive shares.
Under the proposed reorganization Petro-Canada would have the potential of becoming not just the largest Canadian controlled company but perhaps the largest company in the energy field in this country. The performance of management and the board of directors will be measured by the profitability of the resources it has under its control. Direct ownership by Canadians is preferable to assigning responsibility to government officials, with only the electoral process as a periodic control mechanism.
There is no issue that I feel more strongly about than our freedom which exists under the free enterprise system. Our liberty is directly linked to free enterprise. If free enterprise is destroyed we lose our political freedom. If we believe in the freedom of the individual from state domination, we must not allow any government to dominate our economy through government ownership.
Our government intends to give individual initiative the opportunity to flourish once again, and to stimulate the enthusiasm of all Canadians to take a stake and to share in the risks of building a better Canada. It is the creative drive in people, the energy of individual Canadians operating in a free economy where there are opportunities and where government is an assistance, not a hindrance, it is individuals, not bureaucracy, not government, that make a nation great.
I for one will be delighted to own the shares of the new Petro-Canada. If run properly as a commercial operation it will be one of the best investments any Canadian could hold. This is an opportunity for our children and for their children to participate in the immense economic wealth of their country.
In closing, I put the following question to this House. Do you prefer that Canadians own Petro-Canada through their federal government, as they own Air Canada and the post office, or do you prefer that Canadians pay lower taxes and have the opportunity to make their own choice of investment?
