subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I take the floor to speak in the debate on the Speech from the Throne, I recall an extremely pleasant moment I experienced in 1969 when at the request of the then prime minister I had the privilege of seconding a motion for an Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Being aware of the importance of the role we have to assume I take great pleasure in congratulating the movers of the motion for an Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Also I would like to extend my congratulations to the Speaker for his re-election, to assure him of my collaboration and to remind him that probably all members appreciate his competence and his devotion.
First, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the Speech from the Throne must not necessarily contain the detailed list of what the government proposes to do during the session. What is generally expected is a general statement on the direction the government intends to take for a given period, bearing in mind the problems that confront the country. We know that, in this day and age, Speeches from the Throne are often long, that they are made up of general considerations on the state of the nation, the problems it faces and an enumeration of the bills to be submitted to the legislators. In that regard, the Speech from the Throne of October 9 by the new Governor General is more in the old tradition than in the new. It is rather short, possibly even laconic, compared with some speeches of the preceding government.

A Speech from the Throne, whether long or short, specific or vague, always says something by which one can judge to some extent whether the government has the upper hand or not, whether it knows where the country is going, whether it has policies and ideas to offer as solutions to current problems. Now, what is one to think of the first Speech from the Throne of the new government? Its concision betrays at once great wariness and a lack of confidence in itself on the part of this party that accedes to power for the first time in 16 years. This speech confirms what was suspected from the start, that this inexperienced team is still somewhat haunted by the scope of the difficult problems Canada faces at the present time. But, from a government that spent the last few years criticizing the former government mainly for its economic, energy and constitutional policies, the Speech from the Throne clearly indicates that it has yet to make its bed, that it did not make it in those three fields of endeavour.
In the economic sector it announced a series of measures which are certainly warranted to a certain extent, if not entirely original. But we do not have the feeling that the government has an exact idea of the remedy which our condition requires. I see a clear indication of this in the fact that it is counting a lot on the upcoming federal-provincial conference which is to set the economic targets of Canada for the next decade and determine together with the provinces the best means to achieve them.
We should certainly not look down on this concern which proceeds from the best federalist spirit, to involve the provinces in the planning of long-term economic policies. But a government bent on demonstrating leadership must have its own outlook on matters and express it. In any event, it must act and indicate how it intends to act if it wants to inspire the trust which is so necessary for the expected recovery.
Yet, it is in the economic sector that the new government apparently wanted to impress the public most by announcing rather pompously a five-phase strategy. One is undeniable and it concerns once again the control of government activities: expense cutback procedures already announced in Jasper at the end of the summer, staff cuts in the public services, sunset legislation allowing for the termination of government activities which are no longer justified.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw particular attention to a project which means a great deal to the Lac Saint-Jean region and for which its representatives have fought for over three years. When the government speaks of budget cuts, it creates confusion, in my view, maybe not willfully so, but it does create confusion in the minds of the people. For three years, Mr. Speaker, and after heated debate, we have been authorized to build a taxation data center in Jonquiere, and this project might create, in the short or longer term, 1,000 temporary or permanent jobs. In an area where the unemployment
October 18, 1979

rate ranks among the highest in Canada, this project is of crucial and vital importance. 1 urge the government not to take action to stop this project, however short the deadline may be.
The federal government has already directly invested $2 million in this project. The foundations of the building are already built. A contract for construction of the structure has been awarded to the lowest bidder; moreover, and it is important that this be recalled, the city of Jonquiere, at the request of the federal government, has modified its plans for future development in order that the site be rearranged according to the requirements of the federal government and located in the middle of the three former communities of Jonquiere, Kenoga-mi and Arvida, which are now amalgamated under the name of Jonquiere, a building symbolizing the federalism we are advocating on all sides of the House. I must commend most particularly my colleague who is here in the House right now. He was the minister for our area, the minister of regional economic expansion, and he worked hard both within cabinet and in other places so we would have in our region that building which is the most concrete proof to separatists that federalism is not only discussion and dialogue but really jobs we need in an area highly troubled by unemployment reaching alarming proportions which are close to the highest in Canada.
So I would like to say beyond any political partisanship that it is not Gilles Marceau, federal member of Parliament, who is speaking, but the spokesman for a remote area of this great country of ours who is imploring this government-and they will get the credit for continuing that building; I will make sure of it-but I ask them, I beg them nearly on my knees not to delay that construction because there are thousands of people waiting for jobs, trying honourably to earn a living, who are often blamed for being unemployed although it is not always their fault. 1 recall that this government has received a petition from ladies in my riding containing 22,000 signatures. Only women can do interesting and persuading things like that. They went around homes, gathered 22,000 signatures and sent them here to Ottawa. The Jonquiere city council prepared a long brief indicating the investments of over $5 million which have now been made by the city of Jonquiere and the provincial government for the road network, and the federal government has committed $2 million.
The estimates of the Department of Public Works included an amount of $3,500,000 earmarked for the continuation of the work because, as I said, the foundations are there, the plans are practically completed, only the structure is needed and the lowest bidder submitted his price and was accepted. I am not suggesting the government did not have the right to stop that project. I think it is normal for a government to examine each and every project before investing. 1 admit it is their responsibility to see whether the project really meets a need.
I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) during the question period when he said, "we are going to examine which
The Address-Mr. Marceau
projects create jobs, which projects are the most effective". Well, I want to urge him, and I know that he can accept our representations, I urge him and I urge the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Nielsen) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker) to carry on that project. It is not a party which will benefit from that project, it is the people in that area who want it, who require it, and I believe that it is one of their fundamental rights to ask that federalism be advantageous not only for big cities, big centres, but that it be good as well for people who live in remote areas and who are also going to vote in the Quebec referendum. Until the government takes a decision on that matter, 1 think that we are in no position to convince people that federalism is good for them; the project is temporarily stopped and people are beginning to wonder. Still I would not want to voice a definite opinion about this.
I know the government will take into consideration that request 1 make on behalf of the population, on behalf of the 22,000 people who signed the petition, on behalf of the city of Jonquiere which has presented the petition, as well as on my behalf since I presented a memorandum and on behalf of the President of the Treasury Board who has met with those people to discuss this with them.
In addition to those few general remarks on the budget, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that major problems like energy, inflation and unemployment are mostly dealt with in a futile phraseology. The Progressive Conservatives are in turn experiencing the advantages and disadvantages of our status as a U.S. subsidiary, forced to counter the blows as well as we can. The increase in the bank interest rate just struck a hard blow on our economy and thus cancelled the benefits which were to be derived from the mortgage interest deduction program the government should eventually introduce. On constitutional matters, nothing in the throne speech shows a vision of Canada in the future, of the role the federal government should be playing in a country threatened by centrifugal forces. It is noteworthy that it says a lot about diversity in Canada but nothing about the unity to be preserved or restored.
The same thing is true of the energy problem, which is very serious in itself and which moreover threatens to accelerate the political disintegration of our country. Since major Canadian problems have a more or less direct relationship with the main problem of our unity crisis, the government will be unable to implement a coherent and credible energy policy if it does not first define its purpose in constitutional matters. The jewel of the Speech from the Throne should have been the energy policy at which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has worked all summer long and about which he had given us a lot of hope, but there is now a deadlock between Ontario and Alberta concerning the pricing of Canadian oil, and the evasiveness of the Governor General

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Marceau
shows the reluctance of the government to use its arbitration powers since this could damage its general purpose theory of non-confrontation federalism.
Since the price of gas may go up in the near future to $1.30 a gallon and in view of the tragic effects of this increase on those who not only drive their cars but must also heat their homes with oil, since major increases of this importance are foreseen, both sides of the House must concentrate their efforts to try to make a decision at the federal level which will be equitable for everyone and go beyond the individual or collective interests of the provincial governments.
The term "non-confrontation federalism" is an electoral cliche which seems increasingly on the way to becoming a constitutional principle even though it does not exist in practical government. It is useful when provincial interests coincide, for instance in the case of lotteries and provincial offshore resource rights, but it is not sufficient in a case of a conflict of interest. We have only to think about the conference of communications ministers, where the premiers requested yesterday jurisdiction over cable distribution, to which the federal government rightly objected. The provinces have already started to show some impatience and dissatisfaction and they will continue to ask for more as long as the government gives them everything they want. However, I believe they can be responsible enough to realize, when the government refuses their requests, that this disintegration of the central power must come to an end since it has already gone too far in one direction, which does not mean that we should go in the other direction.
The speech outlines a number of legislative measures that appear to be so much less objectionable that their brevity leaves no room for criticism. But one thing above all is lacking in that document-a thrust, a vision, a certain image of tomorrow s Canada that would instil courage and call to action.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to say a few words on the dismantling of Petro-Canada. I know that members opposite have different views from ours. But as far as I am concerned, the point can be made that the hydrocarbons market, especially the oil market is controlled by foreign multinational corporations, and those corporations in the conduct of their business do not give due priority to Canada's national interests. In a period of 40 years, no private Canadian corporation succeeded in achieving a major role in the oil industry. Petro-Canada, a Crown corporation owned by all Canadians, has become in a matter of years Canada's biggest oil company. As I see it, Petro-Canada gave the Canadian government for the first time the expertise vitally needed to really know what is happening in that sector. Like a number of other nations, Canada now has in Petro-Canada an important instrument to better protect our national interests in that industry. I therefore urge the government to consider the situation in depth, to look at the survey showing that 75 per cent of Canadians generally

approve of Petro-Canada. It seems to me that we should keep Petro-Canada as the property of all Canadians and a major instrument of Canadian policy in energy matters.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would once more ask the government, outside of any partisan politics, to decide on a work re-start on the fiscal data centre in Jonquiere. In so doing they will prove to the people in my area that they are a sensible government, and the thousand jobs they will be creating will deserve them praise as they will the previous government who started the project. And for once a genuine link will have been provided between past and present.

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House will know, today marks the fiftieth anniversary of the "Persons case", that historic decision by the Privy Council of Great Britain which declared that women were in fact "persons" and were thus eligible under the British North America Act to "be summoned to and become members of the Senate of Canada". This decision was the result of the tireless efforts of five Alberta women: Emily Murphy, Nellie McClung, Henrietta Muir Edwards, Louise McKinney, and Irene Parlby. It is fitting that the House pay tribute today to the efforts of those five Alberta women, and to the efforts of countless others in the 50 years since the Persons case who have worked to reduce the obstacles to equality for women in Canada.
Seven such women were honoured last evening by His Excellency the Governor General, and the House would want to join in recognition of the rank of Dr. Elizabeth Bagshaw of Hamilton, Ontario; the honourable Therese Casgrain of Montreal; Marion Royce of Toronto, Dr. Grace Maclnnis of Vancouver, Eileen Tallman-Sufrin of White Rock, British
October 18, 1979

Columbia; Mary Two Axe Early of Caughnawaga, Quebec; and Sophia Dixon of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext:
The stark fact, on this fiftieth anniversary of a landmark decision, is that women have not achieved equality-economically, politically, socially.
[ Translation]
Economically speaking, women are second class citizens. Despite a sharp increase in the number of women in the labour force, and considering that it continues to grow, there is always a marked gap between their conditions of employment and those of men, particularly as regards the number of jobs available, the nature of work, the salary, working hours and opportunities for promotion. In the area of employment, women are pushed back in ghettos or in positions characterized by low pay and limited mobility. The gap between the income of men and women is enormous and it widens continually. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the average income of women represents only 53 per cent of the average income of men. And women are most affected by unemployment-9.1 per cent compared to 6.9 per cent for men.
Among senior citizens, women are often alone with a small pension or often with no pension at all. Even with the old age security pension, among single women, widows, divorced women or women over 65, three out of five live under the poverty line.

Politically, women have not achieved equality. One look around this chamber is enough to show that. Socially, a second class status persists, reinforced by the fact that many women-because of their economic dependence-are often powerless to change their situation. Clearly, the situation of women in this country 50 years after the Persons case is not one of which we can be proud. It is a priority of my government that this situation must change. I have spoken many times in the House as leader of the opposition on the failures of government policy in relation to women. Now, as head of a new government, I intend to try to rectify some of those failures and to develop policies that are sensitive to the needs and aspirations of Canadian women.

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext:
We have to remedy the economic situation which follows from the second class status we reserve for women. One of the most important findings of the latest report on women and poverty prepared by the National Welfare Council is the one which says that in most cases women are poor because poverty is the natural consequence of the role society gives them.
Our economic structures leave no room for equal status. To remedy this situation, an important step would be to recognize the influence of the jobs traditionally reserved for women which leads them to poverty and to find solutions to the
Persons Case
problem. We are currently preparing an employment strategy which will deal precisely with this problem.
False solutions intended to bring down the unemployment rate among women by creating short-term jobs will not really improve the employment situation for women. We have to recognize that segregation in employment, lower salaries, limitation of promotion opportunities and care of children are all realities and that we, in the House, have a duty to find solutions to these problems because, in the final analysis, not only women will benefit from them, but the whole society. [English]
An employment strategy for women must be based on two fundamental premises; first, women are in the labour force to stay; second, women have the right to participate in economic activity on the same terms and conditions as men.
The objectives of that employment strategy will include lowering the female unemployment rate through permanent full and part-time jobs, reducing job segregation and developing measures to work toward its eventual elimination, and lowering the wage gap between men and women.
The employment strategy that is presently being drawn up by Status of Women Canada, in conjunction with other departments, will contain measures dealing with women in the public service as well. We will be developing an enhanced equal opportunity policy to advance women in the public service, and developing measures to ensure that the proportion of women in the public service is maintained, and even improved, during the period of attrition.
Once women achieve equality in the work force, they will be able to achieve equality in retirement. But until that goal is reached we must do something to alleviate the extreme poverty among elderly women.

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext:
We have announced a committee inquiry into pension and retirement questions. That committee will consider the pension situation for women. I hope it will make recommendations to the government upon which we can act with some speed.
In the meantime, one of my government's commitments is to cease the practice of cutting off the spouse's allowance upon the death of the pensioner spouse. This is only a first step, but a necessary one, and it is the bill with which we will begin this new Parliament of Canada on Monday next.
In the social realm, the abuse of women both inside and outside the family is something that must be rectified. In this regard we intend to do our part by rationalizing the sexual assault offences and by calling on the provinces to do their part in relation to the administration of justice in the matter of violence against women. In addition, the interdepartmental committee on family violence is working towards a national consultation to find solutions to the problem of family violence, of whom the chief victims are women. This committee was begun under the former government, and I consider its work to be a priority in coming to grips with the problem of violence against women.

October 18, 1979
Persons Case
Finally, in order to end the discrimination in the Indian Act against women who marry non-Indians, we will be bringing in an amendment to amend the discriminatory sections of that act.

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my earnest hope that the women of Canada do not have to wait another 50 years to achieve equality of status with men and to be true persons in our society. We should not have needed the courts to declare in 1929 that women were persons. Nor should we need to be reminded of the fact in 1979.
The hard truth, however, is that women are still not considered full and equal persons, that every inch towards equality has been won only by a hard fight against public opinion, and that a lot of attitudes must change before the goal of true equality is reached.
I hope that the commemoration of Persons Day throughout the country today will mark a beginning in a drastically needed change of attitude, and that in the future such commemorations will be reminders of injustices of the past-and not of the present.

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we on this side welcome many of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Clark) statements today. I join with him in paying tribute to the distinguished women he mentioned at the beginning of his remarks. I noted that he talked about Alberta women, and women from across Canada. I am happy in terms of my parochial interest to thank him for recognizing Dr. Elizabeth Bagshaw. I might say that I too should like to pay tribute to an Alberta woman, a woman I met about 20 minutes ago, a totally charming and disarming woman, and a very friendly one indeed. She happens to be the Prime Minister's mother.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I must say that having met her I feel totally unable to make any unkind remarks, which pretty well necessitates obliterating about three quarters of my speech.
I do wish to pay tribute to the women of Canada on this the fiftieth anniversary of the Persons case. I pay special tribute to those brave Alberta women who led the battle some 50 years ago, but I honour as well all those women who followed them in their determination to create a society where women have an equal place. Since that momentous decision in 1929, which in very narrow terms allowed women to be appointed to the Senate, many changes have taken place in the lives of Canadian women. Many doors have opened, but there is still a long way to go. There are still people in our society who do not enjoy all the benefits of full citizenship, and a great many of them are women.
The problems of our country-inflation, a faltering economy, a high rate of unemployment, and reduced social services-all rest heavily on the shoulders of women. Despite the increasing awareness and more general recognition of women's rights, there are still areas of discrimination and, as society becomes ever more complex, new issues concerning women arise. We must continue as elected representatives to be responsive to the needs of women so ably expressed by women.
The Prime Minister referred to the government's employment strategy. Many of his comments with respect to that were most welcome, but might I point out two principal concerns if any employment strategy is to have a real chance of implementation. One is the key area of day care centres across Canada. Recent statistics indicate that day care centres are on the decrease. Success cannot be attained in terms of equal opportunity for women in the work place if day care centres are inadequate. Lacking such centres, many women cannot take advantage of the opportunities for employment so many of them wish to obtain in order to alleviate the very poverty of which the Prime Minister spoke. I think this is an area in which the Prime Minister would have particular influence with his colleagues in the provinces, many of whom are premiers, and I would hope he would undertake to place that subject on his agenda at the earliest possible opportunity.
The other key to considerably alleviating inequality with respect to women lies in the area of private pensions. A lot could be done there in terms of survivors benefits, early vesting, and indexing. Again in terms of the realization of the objectives the Prime Minister so eloquently spoke of, this topic should be placed high on his priority list for discussion with the provinces as so much of this area falls within provincial jurisdiction. Certainly under the Canada Assistance Plan the federal government can, in co-operation with the provinces, attain a great deal.
The celebrations around the country today reflect the joy and pride we feel on this important anniversary, but the day should also serve to remind us that the work toward a truly equal society, a society where all citizens are full citizens, must continue with renewed force.
I should like to take this opportunity to commend women's organizations both of yesterday and today for their sense of purpose and for their work toward a just Canada. Their record is already an impressive one. May they go on from strength to strength. Many of my hon. friends within this party and on this side feel very strongly on this whole question. I refer to the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), the hon. member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni), the hon. member for Saint Leonard-Anjou (Miss Begin). I hope they will have some appropriate comments to make during this discussion.

Mr. Speaker, it was with a great deal of pleasure that I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) make his statement today commemorating the very important fiftieth anniversary of the Persons case.
As someone who believes strongly in equality for women I compliment the government most heartily on this important

October 18, 1979

public gesture. I would also add in this context that I was pleased to see the recognition given to pioneer Canadian women who contributed to advancing the status of women, in the form of medals presented last night by the Governor General of Canada. 1 know the government is directly involved in those activities as well and it deserves commendation for that action, too.
In this context, and I do not mean it in any partisan sense, 1 was pleased to note that four of the seven women were very active in the cause in which I deeply personally believe. 1 say this given the history of my own party and its forerunner. That, too, is not only a commendation of the women but of the impartiality of the government on this occasion. 1 should like to say in this context that the party I lead in the House of Commons has a long tradition of being concerned with the equality of women, as was recognized last night in those awards. But it is also a continuing battle, and 1 should like to take the opportunity briefly to praise in particular the continuing efforts of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who has fought long and hard for the cause of women throughout the country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext:
Having made these points, I want to go on to make some observations of a rather different nature both in tone and substance. The economic leadership which Canadian citizens were promised by the Prime Minister during the recent election campaign has been, in the main, 1 regret to say, lacking in all areas, including that of the equality of women. The government has already had five months in which to initiate measures to respond to the grave economic crisis which literally thousands of Canadian women face today disproportionately-unemployment and lay-offs, cutbacks in vital support services, and an alarming state of poverty clearly documented by the National Council of Welfare. This is the reality after five months of the present government. 1 regret to say that the Conservative response to this embarrassing situation has chiefly been the recycling of election promises, a few regressive proposals and a few token gestures, in addition to the positive things the Prime Minister mentioned today.
In the main the statement of the Prime Minister which we just heard could have been a carbon copy of the election promises which were outlined in his speech on May 6. At that time he stated:
We believe the most effective role for the federal government in promoting the status of women is to set an example.
I use that quotation to raise and answer the question: has that example really been set in the five months the Prime Minister has had since assuming his important office?

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext: Yes!

subtopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF "PERSONS CASE"-PROPOSED MEASURES TO IMPROVE STATUS
speechtext:
I will offer my view now to hon. members opposite. If this is leadership by example, in my view we will
Persons Case
have to wait another 50 years before full equality of women can be realized!
Let me mention just a few examples of the government's inability to provide serious leadership up to this point, not discounting some of the changes which were announced and which have been long over due. During his presentation to the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women yesterday, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) reaffirmed the Conservatives' election promise to give women a higher priority in Outreach by reinstating some $3 million to the program. That sounds good, but what the minister failed to say yesterday was that he has already admitted that the total budget for women's Outreach projects for this year will amount only to somewhere between $300,000 and $400,000. This paltry sum-and paltry it is for such an important task-will be allocated to only the few women's Outreach programs which survived the Liberal's cutback campaigns of last year.
The point is that the government has simply refused to reinstate worth-while women's projects which were forced to close because of lack of funds, and there are many of them across the country and many which the party in power itself was critical of when it was in opposition, such as Saskatoon's Women in Society Today. Many projects were cut off. They have not been reinstated, and no commitments have been made to any women's Outreach programs for the 1980-81 fiscal year. Surely this is a serious point.
When the government referred to women in the public service, during the election campaign, its members promised that the reduction in the federal public service would have no disproportionate effect on women. Despite this commitment women have continued to be laid off in numbers greater than their labour force participation would indicate, in every single branch of the public service.
Guidelines to ensure that there is no decrease in the number of women working in the public service are simply nowhere to be seen, as was made evident in responses to questions asked by members of my party in the past few days.
Still another election promise was a commitment to:
. . .monitor and recommend changes in public service remuneration scales so that the principle of "equal pay for work of equal value" is effectively applied within the federal service of Canada.
Not only have such recommendations not been forthcoming but, even worse, the government has totally shirked its responsibility in this area. Instead of setting an example for the private sector, the government, as the largest single employer of women workers in the country, is refusing to bargain in good faith with employees in negotiations on the issue of equal pay for work of equal value. If the government is committed to the equal pay principle, why are increasing numbers of female public service employees being forced to take their complaints to the Human Rights Commission? The numbers are increasing daily. I refer the Prime Minister specifically to government librarians, psychiatric nurses, home economists, physiotherapists and occupational therapists, all of whom have had complaints on this principle.

October 18, 1979
Persons Case
At a September meeting the Minister of Employment and Immigration publicly pledged that, and 1 quote, "No new legislation would discriminate against women". In the next breath the same minister admitted that proposed amendments to the unemployment insurance program might include tougher eligibility requirements for voluntary quitters, many of whom will be women who will quit their jobs-and 1 do not exaggerate-because of sexual harassment. Surely that is a legitimate reason for quitting, and a woman ought not to be punished for that if she has contributed to the unemployment insurance scheme. Many will have to quit because their husbands will change the locations of their jobs and move elsewhere. Surely a woman ought not to be penalized under the unemployment insurance system for that.
1 understand also that serious consideration is being given to a two-tiered benefit structure which would directly affect and tie benefits to family composition. This would deprive many women of the benefits to which they are entitled. It is deeply disturbing to me that the Conservative government is even thinking-let alone acting-about introducing a family-based insurance scheme which would virtually cut off benefits to thousands of married women.
I could go on to a number of matters which ought to be pursued by a government which wants to make constructive change beyond matters of tidying up, to which the Prime Minister referred, but I will conclude at this point by saying that this party is deeply and profoundly, both historically and at present, committed to the idea of equality between men and women, and 1 urge the Prime Minister, if he undertakes one commitment in the life of this Parliament-and I mean in the life of this Parliament-to do everything he can within the framework of federal law to bring the goal of full equality between men and women into being in this Parliament.

Prime Minister and the members of his ministry, particularly my fellow Nova Scotian, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), now the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. I will speak more about the necessity of expanding the role of his department in the Atlantic region.
My reference to the Atlantic region reminds me that this area is not always understood by the citizens of other parts of Canada. Often we are regarded by Canadians as a drain on the national economy. But it must be recognized that today many parts of the maritimes, and particularly Nova Scotia, rival the best areas of Canada. The city of Halifax and its surroundings now comprise one of the finest urban areas in North America.
We have in Halifax West two of the most progressive and developing areas in Nova Scotia, Bedford and Sackville; in fact, Bedford will become Nova Scotia's newest town in 1980. Halifax West with its 100,000 residents and 65,000 electors is the largest constituency on the east coast; it has the lowest unemployment rate, the highest per capita income, and the highest percentage of home ownership in eastern Canada. We are not looking for handouts, but we do require incentives and sensible assistance as we seek to develop our physical and human resources. It is in that light that we examine the Speech from the Throne.
Let me say very quickly that we appreciate the substantive matters and the possibility of new directions for Canada indicated in the speech, and I will comment more specifically on these matters. There is, however, a real omission from the throne speech that is of vital concern to me; I have in mind the plight of the Canadian Armed Forces and the public service of Canada.
In the case of the Canadian Armed Forces, their voting record over the years tells the tale. I will dispense with a review of the statistics and simply say that the support they recently accorded members on this side of the House from the

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Crosby
Halifax area was overwhelming. While my colleagues, like the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), have been diligent in their support of the armed forces, we must recognize that we made commitments that now must be fulfilled.
In summary, we undertook to increase the complement of the armed forces from 79,000 to approximately 85,000. We undertook to improve equipment so that our forces could comply with NATO standards. And we must select a new fighter plane and implement a fighter plane acquisition program so that our air element is not embarrassed internationally-
Not the least important of the concerns of the members of the armed forces is their rate of pay. We demand their loyalty and their devotion to duty, but we must recognize that they live in society and must pay for the goods and services in the same way as other citizens. If servicemen and women are to retain their pride in their uniform and in themselves, they must receive adequate compensation.
I am heartened by the statement of the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. McKinnon) that the armed forces would receive a pay increase effective October 1. 1 hope it will be a reasonable one and will not be frittered away by increased rentals and other internal expenses. In the words of our Prime Minister, "There is no higher calling than service to one's country. But the country must support the people who have decided to serve."
Let me also record some remarks in support of the public service of Canada. In the last Parliament members of government engaged in what became known as "public service bashing". After 16 years, during which the government allowed civil service standards to decline and structures to decay, the government turned on its employees and blamed them for the evils of government. Instead of working with representatives of government employees to remove the cancers that had grown within the public service, the former ministers attempted to manipulate the surgeon's knife and they spread havoc among their employees. The cutbacks resulted in the loss of the fisheries laboratory and other productive activities.
It never ceases to amaze me that intelligent men can expect to govern Canada without the assistance of public servants, employees who must be dedicated, capable, and willing to perform their duties. We can only expect a proper return from our public servants if we allow them to bargain collectively for their vital employment terms and if we refrain from abusing our legislative power over them. In this connection I hope and trust our government will not make the same mistake as its predecessor, and that it will not introduce legislation affecting public servants and their employment without consulting their representatives.
I must mention this, Mr. Speaker. We propose to reduce the size of the federal public service. Many public servants recognize there is waste and over-staffing and that the situation must be remedied. I ask the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) to remember that these employees have rights,

and that he should deal with them fairly and with respect for their rights.
I said the Speech from the Throne contained the promise of a new direction of government in Canada. Nowhere can that new direction be better demonstrated than in the matter of regional development and in the field of energy.
With regard to regional economic development, we were told that the mandate of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion would be strengthened by legislation. I will watch for the introduction of this legislation with great interest, and I am sure that interest will be shared by a great many people in Atlantic Canada.
The concept of a department of government to review and rectify regional disparity is valid and viable, but that department must be at the heart of the central government. It must be properly financed, and unfettered by statutory restrictions.
1 believe the current function of DREE is too narrow in scope and is unnecessarily confined by law and legal definition. There must be federal-provincial co-operation, but the requirement for pre-agreement tends to delay the dawn of real economic progress. We must place more faith in the people involved and rely less on their written words. In short, we want expansion and development, not legalistic arguments; action, not words.
I said DREE must be at the heart of government, and that may necessitate the promotion of the minister to the inner cabinet. I am in favour of that for several reasons.
The hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen) reminded his fellow Nova Scotians that he was part of the inner circle of the late Liberal government. He scolded the Prime Minister for not according our Nova Scotia minister the same status. It is true that the hon. member sat by the throne of the former prime minister, but Nova Scotians paid a price for his status. He was singled out for his unselfish ways, for keeping his eye on the national interest; Sydney Steel crumbled, the Donkin coal mines lay undeveloped, the Halifax shipyards were idle and oil supplies were diverted from the east coast, but the procedures of this House were handled with great care and attention. If that is what having the ear of the prime minister does for Nova Scotia, then I suggest our minister stay in the outer cabinet and demand dollars for us instead of dinner parties.
I see that the clock is approaching six, Mr. Speaker. If it pleases Your Honour, I would call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
If the House agrees, it is now six o'clock. It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock this evening.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
October 18, 1979

Mr. Speaker, the evening recess permitted an opportunity to reflect upon my remarks concerning the former member for South West Nova who, as you will recall, 1 said was the first woman elected from the province of Nova Scotia to this chamber. I did not want to imply, nor would I want anybody to infer, that we were not perfectly satisfied with the new member for South West Nova, who also served in this House, I believe, between 1972 and 1974. In no way did I wish to imply that the people of Nova Scotia should consider returning that woman to this House. While she served well, once was enough.
You were right the first time.

I said earlier that the Speech from the Throne contained the promise for new direction of government in Canada, and 1 reviewed the possibility of that direction in the field of regional disparity. I would like to continue my comments on the throne speech and its contents.
We on the Atlantic coast realize that many of our hopes for the future rest with the rapid development of the fishing industry, and we await anxiously the white paper mentioned in the throne speech. We also welcome new developments in agriculture. There is no finer person in this House than the man who now heads that ministry. I know that he will be warmly welcomed in Atlantic Canada. We are also pleased that shipbuilding and the merchant marine will receive special attention from the government.
The Speech from the Throne mentioned the goal of self-sufficiency in energy by 1990 and recognized the role of the provinces in achieving this end. For me, this is a vital challenge for both the national and our provincial governments. If we cannot achieve energy self-sufficiency and acceptable cost burdens, all other economic measures are doomed to failure, and we will lose our quest for improved social and living conditions for all Canadians. Energy self-sufficiency means more than an adequate and secure supply of fuels and generation.
Equally important as the availability of supply is the price we must pay for energy. Energy self-sufficiency will not be achieved in Canada if one part of the nation pays twice the price for gas or petroleum products as another part. Self-sufficiency will be meaningless if Nova Scotians pay twice the price for gas or electricity as other Canadians.
In the late 1950s the national government decided that all Canadians should have medical care and that that care should conform to a national standard. Medicare became a reality. I believe a wise national government would recognize a similar national standard for energy and say that no Canadian should have to pay more than the national average price for the energy he or she consumes. The Nova Scotia government and most Nova Scotians believe our goal should not be limited to energy self-sufficiency on the supply side, but should also extend and include a national average price limitation on the cost side.
The Nova Scotian government under Premier John Buchanan is working to resolve the energy problem in my province,
The Address-Mr. Crosby
and I believe the problem can be resolved with diligence and intelligence, but federal government assistance is required. Premier Buchanan recently announced his energy policy for Nova Scotia. His course of action combines intelligence, common sense and resourcefulness. He has designed an energy system for Nova Scotia that incorporates diversity and flexibility. At the same time it minimizes environmental risk and maximizes social and economic benefits.
Nova Scotia's previous energy policies left the province dependent on foreign crude oil for almost 85 per cent of its energy requirements. The remaining requirements are met by coal and hydro. Taking Canada as a whole, only 44 per cent of the total energy requirement is met by crude oil, and much of that crude oil is provided domestically. Middle East and other world-wide developments have left Nova Scotia with a high cost source of energy and an uncertain one.
The picture becomes clear in relation to domestic and industrial electricity: 65 per cent of electricity is generated with petroleum derived from imported crude. The solution to the problem is equally clear: Nova Scotia must displace foreign crude with Canadian energy sources. To that end Nova Scotia seeks to develop its coal resources. Estimates indicate a coal resource of 3.5 billion tons in various coal fields. In areas ready for immediate development such as Donkin, Cape Breton, there is said to be 2.6 billion tons, with 800 million tons recoverable using current technology. But federal assistance is required.
While coal production is the major thrust in displacing foreign crude, exploration for oil and gas is a major concern and a real hope for the future. Discoveries in the Sable Island area are being assessed, and the tempo of development and exploration in that area must be accelerated.
The activity in Sable Island and other oil exploration prompts me to mention Petro-Canada. The operations of this agency are complex and not easily understood. I endorse the concept of "privatization". Years in government and public service convince me that government must respect those activities that properly belong to the private sector. Nonetheless, the research activities formerly sponsored by PetroCan must be continued. If they are not, all Canadians will suffer but, in the east, we will suffer more. The report of the task force on PetroCan has indicated this vital work of exploration will continue.
In this connection, Nova Scotians applaud the turnover of offshore mineral rights to the provinces. This does not mean the federal authority cannot play a role in exploration and development. It does give the coastal eastern provinces a chance to achieve a new financial economic status.
At present, utilization of Canadian oil and gas resources involves a serious transportation problem for east coast provinces. Marine transport of Arctic gas is being considered, and a proposal for an east coast pipeline is now before the National Energy Board. These developments are being carefully monitored by the Nova Scotia government.

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Daudlin
More imaginative solutions to energy problems include the development of Fundy tidal power and research activity in coal gasification. The economics of processing coal to liquid fuel is being vigorously pursued. These ventures require immediate federal attention and aid. The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), in his usual thoughtful way, described in detail the possibility of employing peat and other natural fuels to displace expensive foreign crude. His suggestion deserves attention. We would like to see the Annapolis River tidal project implemented immediately.
The challenge in the Speech from the Throne and the challenge for Canada and Nova Scotia is clear: we must solve the energy problem. I am confident that Premier Buchanan and the Nova Scotia government are on the right road to meet that challenge. I am equally confident the Prime Minister will assist us to deal with the energy problem. He has spoken in this House and elsewhere about the necessity of rectifying the economic imbalance in Canada. He understands federal-provincial relations. He recognizes the special needs of Atlantic Canada.
Changing the direction of government in Canada means providing the kind of assistance that leads to self-reliance and self-sufficiency. That is what we want in Nova Scotia, and with this new direction that is what we can achieve.

Mr. Speaker, I hear some of my friends on the left indicating that this is perhaps my maiden speech. 1 suspect those friends were here during the last Parliament but they must have absented themselves from the House for a long, long time, otherwise they would have heard me speak from time to time.
Stanley never hangs in.
You look so young.

It is because I look so young, and it is out of envy that they say that, I think.
It is a distinct honour to be able to participate in this first debate of this Parliament. Like those before me, I would like to congratulate Mr. Speaker on having been chosen once more by this chamber to represent us. As a member who now finds himself on this side of the Speaker's chair, albeit temporarily I am sure, your presence in the chair will afford me an even greater opportunity to benefit from the keen wit and wise judgment referred to earlier by members of this House. I intend to avail myself of those qualities often.
1 join with other members who have participated in this debate in extending my compliments to the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) for their contributions in moving and seconding the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I should as well, by way of preamble to my comments this evening, express my appreciation to the electors of Essex-Kent for their reaffirmation and confidence in my ability to serve their interests in this Parliament. I believe I share with other members of this House the combined pride and humility that

follow from being chosen one of the relatively few spokesmen for the entire population of Canada.
Following the redistribution which took effect on the dissolution of the last House, the constituency which I now represent lost the community of Chatham in the northeast, and with it the substantial urban population which had brought the balance of an urban oriented citizenry to an essentially agricultural riding. With the loss of Chatham the riding has gained an almost totally agricultural area by acquiring two townships, Harwich and Colchester South, together with the larger communities of Blenheim and Harrow. I would be remiss if I did not welcome those new areas to the riding.
As I have indicated, the riding of Essex-Kent is now predominantly rural, with abundant agricultural activity, which included most recently the hosting of the International Plowing Match. This was officially opened by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise). Because of the agricultural nature of the riding one might expect, and I would go further and suggest my constituents would have cause to be disappointed if I did not examine closely the Throne Speech to find how it proposes to deal with so important and vital a part of our economy as agriculture and the production of food.
I listened attentively to the Speech from the Throne when we were in the other place. I examined and re-examined the written copy of the Speech from the Throne, bearing in mind that the present government had taken great pains to put itself on record during the last election as stating that it was the direct and continuing responsibility of a federal government to support the agricultural industry aggressively. Yet, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding meticulous examination of the throne speech and the avowed commitment of that government during the most recent campaign, what I find is that essentially there has been an omission to mention agriculture in the throne speech. One would have to look elsewhere to find any statement of continuing commitment on the part of the Prime Minister or his cabinet to producers of food in this nation.
I cannot overlook either the fact that when the Prime Minister, in putting together his new cabinet, thought so little of his party's commitment, oft repeated during the campaign, of high profile and high importance to the agricultural sector, he opted while selecting those of the inner and those of the outer cabinet to decide that in fact the Minister of Agriculture should be relegated to a position of secondary importance, which neither the Minister of Agriculture nor the people of this nation, and particularly the agricultural producers should be prepared to accept.
The Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, has said that it is time to quit fighting the last election and to move on. But I believe it is important, if we are to determine where this government may be wanting to go, given that it has failed to provide us with a blueprint or plan of action for agriculture in the throne speech, that we look at what that party, through its representatives, was heard to say in the campaign.
The promises were many, Mr. Speaker. They promised they would bring in new ideas and new initiatives to the federal agricultural policy. In fact the Minister of Agriculture, when
October 18, 1979

he was critic of that portfolio, put himself on record in this House as stating, for instance on milk policy, that the import quota on cheese in this country should be reduced by some 10 million pounds at the very least. And yet in his first actions in dealing with that very dairy policy, the minister and his government has not included any such action in any announcements that I am able to find. But he has indicated in some talks that he had privately with some producers elsewhere in the nation that it would perhaps still be a good idea to reduce those imports. And yet when one discusses this with officials, one determines no such action is planned. It leads one to the conclusion that, having assumed the reins of power, they may have now decided that, in fact, the previous administration was correct in the levels which had been set and that no reduction should take place, or alternatively they are unprepared to accept the consequences of reducing the quotas to a level to which they claim to be philosophically committed.
At another time, Mr. Speaker, the representatives of the government suggested that they would be working toward reduction of the escalating costs of farm inputs, including machinery, fertilizer, interest rates and so on, in order to lower the cost of production. Those were the promises, but what have been the actions? Machinery prices have not gone down; they have gone up, and will go up further if, in fact, the energy cost increases proposed by this government are allowed to take place. The cost of fertilizer has not gone down; it has gone up and, indeed, the level of future prices can only be speculated upon if one is to assume that natural gas will be linked to the relative costs of other oil-based energy. One can only cringe at the thought of the possible cost of a bag of nitrate in the spring of 1980.
Then, of course, there is the matter of interest rates, Mr. Speaker. If it were not so serious it would almost be funny. I can recall sitting on the other side of the House and listening to the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), then critic, arguing long and hard-one thought then without much real commitment to the idea, but with a healthy dose of partisanship-that increase after increase was wrong, that it would lead to inflation, that it would have a detrimental impact on the lives of the people of Canada, that it should be fully discussed by Parliament before being allowed to take place, that the minister should not slavishly follow the dictates of the governor of the Bank of Canada, and indeed, the movements of the industry in the United States.
Now what has happened, Mr. Speaker? Conversion, a seeing of the light! Perhaps they have accepted that it was the right thing to do. Now they seem to argue that it was wrong then and right now. In any event, they seem to have a renewed faith in the Bank of Canada and a sudden inspirational understanding of what has happened for the last three years. It is almost enough to shake one's confidence. But as bad as those things are, they do not hold a candle to something else. And indeed, maybe all that we are going to have left for light in this country is candles if, in fact, this government is allowed
The Address-Mr. Daudlin
to continue to do what it proposes to do by way of PetroCan and the petrochemical industry.
It would now appear that they have reached a decision to move immediately, precipitously and, in my view, unthinkingly towards world prices, regardless of the cost of replacement, regardless of the cost necessary to assure exploration, and regardless of the cost of production. Perhaps I could stand by and I could argue against it, and perhaps I could almost argue detachedly were it not for the fact that I am so completely convinced of the incredible impact, yes, the incredible, detrimental impact that this will have on the food production industry in this nation.
The previous administration, in an attempt to assure continued supply and continuity of supply, in an attempt to move prices upward, while buffering and cushioning the Canadian public from the adverse effects of abrupt changes upward in oil pricing that had been experienced throughout the world as a result of OPEC decisions, saw input costs in the agricultural sector increase dramatically, and I have heard, and members of this House have heard the reasons for those increases.
Many have accepted them and others have argued that it was wrong. But they were accepted, they were imposed, they were lived with, and the farmers of this nation were put into a cost squeeze that has reached crisis proportions. The agricultural industry is one industry that cannot conveniently pass on its input costs to the consuming public. If and when it does, the impact on the consumer of increased prices for food results in CPI figures like were announced today, showing this nation once again moving toward and shortly into double digit inflation.
Only a few short years ago one of the least concerning input costs in agriculture may have been energy. I suggest, as I attempted only last week to point out in my questions to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and the Minister of Agriculture, that the time has now arrived when the agricultural producers of this country must be given absolutely clear and unequivocal assurances by this government that they are wanted, that they are needed, that, in fact, this government is going to give the assistance necessary to assure their continued existence and is going to provide mechanisms that will protect them against the rising costs of energy as it relates to the cost of the production of food.
So that there can be no confusion, and so that members of this House may understand that I am not spreading alarm unduly, that I am not creating a false crisis, let me offer some examples. In 1971 in Canada the farming community spent $264,708,000 on petroleum, diesel oil, and lubricants for machinery. By 1978 for the same products the price had risen to $519,600,000. Another important statistic to remember is that primary agriculture alone accounts for about 3 per cent of all the energy consumed in this country.
Getting a little closer to home, let me point to the greenhouse industry, one of the most energy intensive industries in this country, an industry worth in Essex county alone some $20 million per year in gross production on a direct basis, without taking into account the salaries involved in packing, in

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Daudlin
transportation, in sales-an industry that has been threatened by the moves that are taking place. Some 62 per cent of the input costs for the production of food in these greenhouses goes to heat them.
There are growers in that constituency, in that industry, who in 1973 were paying 15 cents per gallon for light oil. Two days ago those same growers were paying 59.78 cents per gallon, an increase of almost 400 per cent. At the same time you must recognize that the actual return to the producer for those same crops in gross terms has not yet even doubled. One can immediately comprehend the nature and the extent of the problem. I do not think I overstate the case by suggesting that if in fact the kind of price increases that this government is now contemplating are allowed to take place, they would destroy the greenhouse industry. That $20 million industry in the county of Essex, and the extension of that industry is found in Kent county, in Lambton county, and indeed in the riding of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) as well as in the Niagara peninsula, will find itself hard pressed, and in fact impossible to continue.
It was for that reason 1 raised the question last week. In fact I have had meetings with the Minister of Agriculture since that time. I do not propose merely to point at the problem. I do not propose to suggest that in fact it is a terrible thing and somebody has to do something about it. I have suggested to the ministers, both in the House and privately, that there is a solution to this difficulty that this industry is in the throes of experiencing. I would almost say I have implored those ministers to consider the possibility that if in fact they are going to proceed as a government with the kind of price increases they are talking about, that the agricultural industry as a whole, and the greenhouse industry specifically, should be exempted from those increases.
How that could and should be done would be to fix the cost of energy as an input cost in food production at the level which it was in the spring of 1979, by way of returns, after application and indication by the growers that they were in fact true food input costs. This would be much the way in which we now deal with the situation for taxation on gasoline for farm vehicles. In the same manner the growers should be allowed to make application to the Department of National Revenue for rebates that would sustain the level of their energy input costs for the production of their food at the levels they were at in 1979, which 1 think most members will agree are already high enough to make it very difficult for even a good grower. I suggest that some consideration be given by the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Agriculture to a mechanism such as that, or to some other mechanism which would accomplish the same end.
The only way in which we shall be able to maintain the agricultural industry in general and the greenhouse industry in particular, which in the past has had to sustain too great an impact in terms of energy policy, would be through the adoption of a proposal of this kind. The impact of rising prices

for diesel fuel, nitrates used for the production of fertilizer, and natural gas used for heating, including, particularly, the heating of greenhouses, will be such that producers will not be able to pass it on to consumers because, if they were to do so, the cost of the basic food basket which goes to make up the CPI would send us into a frightening inflationary spiral. 1 am sure none of us in this House wish to see either producers or consumers placed in a position where they are unable to protect themselves.
In the early production years of the Alberta oil fields the greenhouse industry in Essex County was made to pay higher prices for oil than it would otherwise have been obliged to pay if there had been access to the offshore oil then available to areas of Quebec through the Port of Montreal. In the early fifties the consumers of Ontario, and particularly agricultural consumers, were paying prices for oil higher than world prices so that sufficient moneys could be diverted to the Alberta oil industry to enable that industry to be sustained and developed. The producers in my riding are now saying: "Isn't it odd that we should have been made to pay those prices and sustain those costs for the benefit of Albertans in the fifties and now, when we are seeing greenhouses going up for sale and lacking buyers, the oil producers are calling for more and more and more?"
Mr. Speaker, I do not only plead with this government which appears bent upon a policy of increasing those prices. I look beyond this government to the premiers of the provinces which are producing this energy, and ask them to remember and consider what consumers did for them some years ago. I believe 1 must go beyond this government because it seems to be bent on bargaining with the price of energy in order to obtain the consensus it hopes to achieve. It appears, though, if reports are to be believed, that such a consensus will be elusive indeed.
I would not want, by reason of the emphasis I have placed on the energy matter, to leave this House with the impression 1 feel the only agriculturally oriented policy which should have been touched upon by the government in the Speech from the Throne should be concerned with energy and its impact on the cost of production of food. There are other areas that the government should, in my view, have addressed in the Speech from the Throne if it was anxious to provide assurances to the food producers of the nation that there continues to be, and will continue to be, a place for them in the economic fabric of Canada.
The minister said much outside the House in the course of pronouncements during the campaign about the Farm Credit Corporation. In various statements while he was opposition critic he was most supportive of that corporation. Indeed, he has spoken in quite favourable terms of the need to provide new funding sources. But he appears to have taken little or no action since the government came to office to turn his commitment into actions. Perhaps this would not be so bad, in the circumstances, were it not for the fact that there continues to be difficulty in funding farm credit.
October 18, 1979

Right at this time of the year young farmers, attempting to get loans to purchase new farms which they can ill-afford to buy at the present bank rate, find the Farm Credit Corporation saying, "We would love to take your application, but of course you must realize that it will be taken purely upon the basis of our being able to fund it next year when we hope to have more money." It alarms me to read in a newspaper. The Ottawa Journal of October 12, that this corporation, one which persons like myself which represent agricultural areas have always wanted and always been willing to support, should be suggesting it wishes to move into the direction of privatization, as seems to be the aim of the government, and in so doing to remove the competitive advantage which was given it to ensure that it does, in fact, make money available to young farmers in Canada who are trying to buy land at prices that are spiralling out of sight, leaving them in a position where they could not reasonably expect to get that other 200 acres of land, or 300, or 500 or what-have-you.
It is indeed alarming to find that the Farm Credit Corporation, through its chairman, should feel that its competitive advantage over the banks should be reduced, leaving the corporation and the banks on roughly the same ground. This seems to me to go directly against the fundamental principles upon which the FCC was instituted in the first place and it scares me, frankly, when I think of those young farmers in my riding who are finding it ever more difficult to buy land at $6,000 or $7,000 an acre.
In my view it is essential that the Farm Credit Corporation should be given legislation which would allow it to go for funding to sources other than the Treasury Board. It has always lacked that capacity and I, for one, would be prepared to support the Minister of Agriculture as far as possible from this side of the House to ensure that action is taken quickly along those lines in order that farmers should have access to those funds so as to get into the production of food.
If it seems I am being overly persistent in these matters it is only because I have seen no indication by the new government of its stand on any of these vital questions. I might refer to the area of research and development in the agricultural sector. It is of the utmost importance that a country with such bountiful land, land capable of being even more productive, should develop it to the fullest extent, to the benefit not only of ourselves but of the world where far too many people are dying of malnutrition and starvation. It is imperative that there be a strong endorsement and encouragement of research and development in all areas of food production and distribution. The realization of Canada's future agricultural potential must be achieved by advances in skill, techniques, and expertise.
I would be remiss if I did not express the sentiments of the majority of the members of this House-yes, even hon. members opposite-that the hon. member who previously occupied the post of minister of agriculture was viewed very warmly by members of this House and by the producing communities across this nation who, for the most part, were satisfied that
The Address-Mr. Daudlin
great achievements were made in agriculture through the efforts of that man. Regardless of what achievements were made, valuable time has been lost since the election, and such absence of progress in changing times is regression.
The previous administration fought hard to achieve negotiated settlements of bilateral trade agreements on horticultural products for the fruit and vegetable crop producers of this nation. I can but hope and urge very sincerely that substantial priority be given by the government to re-introducing and bringing forward appropriate legislation which would allow the implementation of the bilateral negotiations and assure for producers the guarantees and advantages achieved by those negotiations.
I am particularly worried about the rumours we hear that certain segments of a bilateral agreement are being bartered away and that we may now be seeing certain interest groups in the country suggesting to the government that tariffs on tomato paste, for instance, should be removed because there is not currently a tomato paste industry. We negotiated and fought for seven years.
We tried to obtain for the producers of this nation the kind of tariff protection which now exists in that bilateral agreement and which would have created a milieu in this country which would induce new industry and bring to Canada its own tomato paste industry for consumers of that product in Canada. It also would have put Canada on the map in terms of international production of tomato paste. 1 think all of us knew that that would not happen and could not come about unless and until we had in place the kind of guarantees which would assure companies the opportunity to come, to start off well, and to be able to stay. Having achieved that, we now hear that there are those who would have the government remove those tariffs because the industry is not yet here. 1 argue as strongly as I can that the alternative to that is not to remove but to allow a remission until such time as the new industry is here.
Because there is no Canadian industry, in my view to remit is fair. To remove entirely what has been so hard fought for by producers would be throw our hands up and say we never want to see a Canadian tomato paste industry. I think this has to be dealt with quickly. The uncertainty which now surrounds this matter has to be removed, and we have to indicate that the government is committed to the introduction of such a new industry to Canada.
I would like to suggest to the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance that it might be appropriate on the fiftieth anniversary of the "persons" decision, under which women were considered persons within the definition of the BN A Act for purposes of their selection and entry to the Senate, that those ministers consider the plight today of women involved in agriculture and small business who, by reason of lack of incorporation, find themselves in the position of being integral parts of the farm or small business unit, putting in untold hours of labour on tractors and combines, or perhaps behind the counters of small businesses, and unable to draw salaries which would otherwise be paid to non-spouses or

non-family and, alternatively, if salaries are drawn, receiving money which cannot validly be deducted as expenses.
I believe it is time that this inequity was removed. Fifty years should have been long enough to afford us the opportunity to work out mechanisms which would allow such inequities to be removed from our taxation legislation so that all persons involved in agriculture and small business could receive and have deducted fair compensation for the valuable work they do.
