Mr. Speaker, I count it an honour, a privilege, and a challenge to have been elected to this House by the people of the constituency of Bow River, and I am very happy to take part in this debate.
At the outset I wish to congratulate the mover and the seconder on the splendid addresses they both delivered. Their material was excellent, and their presentations were clear and eloquent.
The Bow River riding is a new constituency. It is made up roughly of 30 per cent of three former constituencies, Palliser, Rocky Mountain, and Crowfoot, with the balance coming from the Lethbridge constituency. The Bow River constituency has virtually everything. It has one of the seven wonders of the world, Lake Louise, and some of the most talked about tourist items in Canada, including the townsite of Banff, nestled in the majestic mountains, and the city of Drumheller, located in the Canyon of the Red Deer where there are the dolomites which have been photographed probably more than most other geological formations in the world.
The three areas, Lake Louise, the Banff townsite and Banff National Park, and the Drumheller areas, are tourist areas extraordinary and draw people from all over the world. The Drumheller valley contains the famous Badlands where the dinosaurs used to roam.
Still do.

They are not quite as fossilized as some of the members of the NDP.
The rock and soil formations attract geologists from all over the world and form the northeast part of the riding. The constituency completely encircles the city of Calgary. There are cattle, horse and sheep ranches, grain farms, poultry farms, oil wells and gas wells. There are scores of small businesses, and there are coal mines. Some businesses are large, some medium, and some small. Bow River is an agricultural, industrial and commercial centre in the thriving province of Alberta.
However, the best thing about the constituency is its wonderful people who come from all countries of the world. They have brought with them their cultures and are making their cultures part of the great Canadian mosaic. The cultures of our native people are found on the three reserves within the riding, the Blackfoot Reserve, the Stony Reserve, and the Sarcee Reserve. All together these people contribute to making Canada a better place in which to live.
On top of all that we have the town of High River, the birthplace of our innovative and energetic Prime Minister (Mr Clark).
Hear, hear!

His parents still live there, and they are wonderful people. Everyone in Bow River and, indeed, in Alberta, is proud of the fact that a native son has become the Prime Minister of this great country, and under his leadership our country will become united and strong. I am proud to have the opportunity to represent such wonderful people and such a wonderful constituency.
One of the thrilling paragraphs in the Speech from the Throne reads as follows:
My ministers were given a mandate to change the direction of the Government of Canada, as we enter the 1980s. The basic purposes of that change will be to enhance the rights, freedoms and opportunities of individual Canadians, and re-establish the spirit of partnership and renewal which are fundamental to our federation.
"To change the direction of the Government of Canada" that is the reason the Progressive Conservative Party is on this side of the House. Why did the people of this nation want a change of direction? Well, let us look at just a few items. For ten or more years free enterprise values which made Canada a healthy, inventive and prosperous country have been discredited. There has been a mulligan stew of collectivism and statism. Government ownership permeated legislation, and then the administration crippled free enterprise by regulating and controlling the economy. The government told the people what was good for them, leaning more and more to the left, and with the help of the NDP they tried to kill free enterprise altogether.
Now they are getting closer and closer.

Yes, they are getting closer together every day. As a result, people became afraid to invest money in their own country and they invested elsewhere. More than $2 billion left Canada since 1974. Besides torturing the productive system of this country, they went on a wild spending spree spending money they did not have to the tune of billions of dollars. In 1973 Canada had a small surplus on current account in its international trade and payments account. By late 1974 and every year thereafter our current account deficit was around $4 billion or more. It was an extremely poor performance. The Canadian dollar declined from $1.03 in 1976 to about 83 cents in terms of the U.S. dollar, a fall of nearly 20 per cent by 1979. Depreciation of our

October 18, 1979

dollar against currency such as the Japanese yen, the West German mark and the Swiss franc was almost 40 per cent, but even this was not enough to make any substantial improvement in the trade balance.
To add to the dilemma, this resulted in almost one million people becoming unemployed, fewer goods were produced, the gross national product was below that of the United States, below that of Japan and below that of France. As a result inflation became rampant. The government of the day continued to spend more than it had, and the government deficit grew to as much as $13 billion. The deficit in the balance of payments grew to over $5 billion. But deficits had to be paid, and so the government went outside the country to borrow money, leaving a legacy of debt that generations yet unborn will have to pay because of this economic mess that was created.
No wonder the interest rate rose seven times in a few months during the last weeks of their administration, and now the Liberals have the audacity to ask why the interest rate is increasing. They know that the deficit must be covered by an equal amount of capital coming into the country. So long as this economic mess continues, it will be chaotic to have the flow of capital going out of Canada until we are at least able to get production up to a point where there will not be too many dollars chasing too few goods. Yes, the economic mess was created by the Liberals and we are still living with it. It cannot be cured over night. Instead of playing politics, I would think the Liberals today would assume responsibility for the mess in which they left this country, the mess that our present government is trying to clean up.
In 1968 the debt of this country was some $32 billion, and for this we paid annually more than $1 billion in interest. That was bad enough, but within the next ten years of the Liberal administration under its present leadership, the debt grew to $80 billion-more than double. The people of Canada were paying almost $7 billion in interest every year.
The former minister of agriculture said the other day that he left Canada in a good state. A good state? A messy state, if I know anything. In addition to that, there was a flight of more than $2 billion out of this country to build industry and to provide jobs in other countries, while our own people were unemployed. The gross national product was not growing. Trade deficits were continuing to grow larger each year. It is fortunate indeed that Canada has not gone into complete bankruptcy. As a matter of fact many people said to me, as I knocked on their doors in Bow River, "If that administration is returned, the whole country will be bankrupt." Look at the facts. They had something on which to base their fears. Does anyone believe that the direction should not be changed? Surely it does not take anyone with more than a grade three education to see that something had to be done to clean up this mess into which we were getting deeper and deeper.
Certainly the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) cannot press a button and find that, presto, everything turns rosy. Remember that the country is close to a crisis financially and economically. Even though faced with
The Address-Mr. G. Taylor
this economic mess, the Progressive Conservative government is determined to turn the crisis into an opportunity to give free enterprise a chance to work, to create a climate where people will be glad to invest their money in their country, not send it elsewhere, and a chance to free our industries and our people from the regulatory bondage in which they have been placed.
Hear, hear!

Wealth comes not from government offices or politicians' edicts but from that portion of the market place which is free. Collectivism, centralized planning, regulation after regulation, frustrate people to the point where they will not even bother investing their money. One man said to me, "It is so hard to invest $100,000 in this country. I am going down to Florida where I can invest the money and where people are glad to have the investment." That man can come back to Alberta and to Canada because there is not going to be this red tape that tries to keep people from investing in their own country.
The multinational companies have their place. They provide employment, and as good corporate citizens they should pay their share of running this country and give our workers a fair return for their labour. Along with the multinationals we need hundreds of thousands of individuals in partnerships, small businesses working for profit in a free market. What will the result be? The result will be interacting individual decisions with no conscious direction from the government, no single purpose for each goal. Each individual has his own purpose and goal and seeks to secure the greatest reward to avoid or to cut his losses or to make a contribution. There are literally thousands of purposes, millions of decisions and millions of adjustments every day as inventors, entrepreneurs, middle men, employers, workers, buyers and sellers pursue their own prospective interests for themselves and their families, the sum total of which builds a nation.
Our wonderful neighbours to the south built a nation on the principles of free enterprise and individual freedom. Today they could be energy sufficient had their administration in the last few years not shackled free enterprise. Exploration for coal, oil, uranium, natural gas, came almost to a standstill in that great nation to the south. The administration was tying it up with red tape. The administrations thought they could regulate and control and that free enterprise would still work. The Congress of the United States has been told repeatedly that there is no shortage of fuel as such but that it takes money to find it. Individuals and companies need motivation to invest their money, and a reasonable return is essential. There are vast deposits of coal, oil and gas today in the United States, and I say they would have been self-sufficient had they not allowed the left wing of their party to dictate their policies.
Hear, hear!

Similarly the Liberals emphasized the left wing of their party. I know there are some free enterprisers in the Liberal party and there are some also in the

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. G. Taylor
NDP. Why do they want to shackle free enterprise? Let them come over to this group which breeds free enterprise.
Elear, hear!

Yes, we plan to change the direction in this country.
Now, let us look at another item, namely, tourism. I mention tourism because it can become a great industry in this country. This year, in calculating the amount of money spent by Canadians in other countries, compared to what those who came to Canada spent in Canada, we find a $2 billion deficit. Canada has all its wonders, majestic mountains in Banff and Jasper. There is the wonder of the world in Lake Louise, Eloodoos and dolomites near Drumheller in the badlands of the canyon of the Red Deer River, just to mention a few attractions in my own constituency and to say nothing about the wonders found in the maritimes, Ontario and Quebec. There are wonderful falls in the Northwest Territories. Canada has wonder after wonder, yet we have a $2 billion deficit. Did the former administration ever ask why? I am very happy that the new minister in this government responsible for tourism is taking a look at new directions. We want our people to travel across the country. We must make it attractive for them to do so, in order to keep our money in our country. But that is not the only point. We can do something else as well.
There is a tremendous market for international tourists who would like to come and enjoy the beautiful scenery and wonderful hospitality of Canada. Major tour wholesalers in the United States, Australia and the Pacific rim countries are sending hundreds of people who want to come to Canada to other places, because we have become so bound with red tape in parts of this country that we have not provided accommodation.
Plow would one like to go to the Banff National Park or Lake Louise and find when one got there that there was no place to sleep, and then have to drive 100 miles or more into British Columbia or back to Calgary to find a room? People who have had to do that say they will never come back. Private enterprise today can and would provide accommodation in Banff and Lake Louise, and protect the environment, if given an opportunity to do so. But because of the bureaucracy built up by the previous government, along with the rules and regulations, they cannot do it. They cannot build new motels. They cannot tear down old ones and build modern cabins. The bureaucracy in Parks Canada has become God. They know best what the people want.
A man wanted to start a medical practice in Lake Louise when the Liberals were in power, but they would not let him. People can get sick. In this case the doctor finally became frustrated and left. Bureaucracy has taken hold. The people in the offices think they know what is best. They will not even license a man who wants to work in that particular area. They say that there is some rule or regulation passed by the former

administration which makes it impossible for them to do it; they do not want to break the law.
We want more and more people to come and enjoy the beauty of our mountains, the beauty of the maritimes, the beauty of every province in the country, each one with its unique attractions. Let us encourage entrepreneurs to build accommodation and at the same time protect the environment in our national parks. We should encourage thousands of these internationals, people from other countries, to come and enjoy our scenery. Such a policy will bring in new dollars and help our balance of trade, as well as provide jobs for people. Also it will enable entrepreneurs to provide a different type of traffic which will help the environment. They could provide a bus which would take 60 people instead of 30 cars taking the same number of people, to beautiful Lake Louise. The same thing could apply to other parks across the country.
I speak about Banff National Park because that is part of my constituency. It illustrates what is going on in other parts of the country. There is no end to what can be done to change the direction and turn the travel deficit into a surplus. Capital is waiting to be used if we turn out the red light and turn on the green.
Hear, hear!

I want to say a word or two about agriculture. Certainly agriculture needed some changing, with all due respect to the former minister. To put it in a nutshell, we found a dismal record. There were 2,000 boxcars which were unserviced, 4,000 new hopper cars were required, and 5,000 boxcars needed refurbishing. There was loss of markets. There were approximately 16 ships waiting in Vancouver to be loaded. Western farmers were paying fines of up to $5,000 a day which came out of the pockets of the producers, because the ships had to sit and wait and wait. The nation had a 35-million bushel backlog in exports. It was an all-time high. Producers saw their markets disappearing and going to other countries. They wanted a change of direction. Already we can see the change of direction. There is a changed attitude toward hopper cars entirely. Also I hope we can give the producers of this country a fair return for their products. It has been too long. Every other industry receives its costs plus a reasonable profit. Farmers work for the good of the country. They are entitled to a fair return plus the cost of their labour and a reasonable profit. I hope to see a change in that area during the life of this Parliament.
I should like to deal with another area in which we want to change the direction, and that is the supplying of energy in the country by way of coal. For many years our coal mines remained virtually idle while we bought coal from other countries. Canada has a tremendous tonnage waiting to be mined, yet Canada is a net importer. Year after year the Alberta legislature passed resolutions urging the federal government to assist us in getting markets for our coal. But what happened? In the Drumheller Valley 20 mines disappeared. Only one mine remains. Their market has disappeared. At the same time Canada is bringing in millions of tons of coal from
October 18, 1979

another country. Our own miners are being dislocated and are required to find work after being in the pits and the bosom of the earth for 30, 40 or 50 years. The same thing happened in the province of Nova Scotia. Many of its miners came west and are still working in mines that are operating. But what about the thousands of people who could not find work?
In 1978 15 million tons of coal valued at $750 million were exported; 18.5 million tons valued at $200 million were used in Canada; and 15.5 million tons valued at $660 million were imported into Canada. That was in 1978 when our unemployment level was growing close to the million mark. I was raised in a coal mining community and worked in the mines. My father and my brothers were coal miners. I know what it means to be hungry when the mines had no work. I remember many times coming out of the mines and just yearning to see the light come on in the tipple indicating that there would be work the next day. Around the tables in the homes in the mining area of Newcastle people would say, "If we could only get just a little bit of that Ontario market". Think of the jobs this would have provided, think of the effect this would have had on our balance of trade, think what this would have done toward attaining energy efficiency and sufficiency.
The producers of coal in Canada are the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. There may be coal in other provinces as well. Now there are about ten mines operating in these five provinces, plus two dozen corporations, mostly oil and gas companies, which have sizeable coal rights and are planning to produce coal for conventional uses. Our coal mines should operate for additional domestic and foreign markets. In the province of Ontario we need more than the 3.7 million tons of thermal coal a year to which it is presently committed. I thank the Ontario government for at least giving us a bite of its market. With some help from the federal government, I am sure the people of Ontario will give us more business.
By 1980 the demand for domestic coal is expected to increase greatly. To enable coal to play a meaningful part in our energy requirements, as we work toward self-sufficiency, we need to do certain things. We need additional transportation and terminal capacities. We need to do something about transportation costs.
Research should also play a part as coal can be used in many ways. There are literally a thousand items that can be made from coal. There is a tremendous opportunity in the liquefaction of coal to produce a large range of liquid and gaseous hydrocarbons, and in the gasification of coal to produce low, medium and high Btu gases for combustion; process energy to congeneration of electricity, petrochemical feed stocks, and the manufacture of synthetic fertilizers. There is opportunity for the use of coal as an energy source to recover large amounts of synthetic, heavy oils and bitumens. I have said for years, and I said when 1 was part of the government of Alberta, that we should not be using our oil and our gas, particularly our gas, in our industries. Why do they not use
The Address-Mr. G. Taylor
coal and save the clean fuel for the heating of our homes? Gradually people are coming around to believing that that is right. There is a large range of uses for coal.
Again we should protect the environment, but let us not stop coal mining because a few extreme environmentalists say it is going to hurt the environment. Yes, we should change the direction and produce our own coal when we have such abundant supplies.
There is another item that has been mentioned to me many times as I knocked on doors in the Bow River constituency, and that is the direction in which we are going with the metric system. It was brought into this country in a questionable way by the Liberal administration. This is another example of the former government telling the people what was good for them without the people having an opportunity to have their day in court.
This government believes in reflecting the thinking of the people to the greatest possible degree. Because metric was brought in the way it was, because it is ahead of its time, because the United States is reluctant to go ahead with metric, and because the United States is our greatest trading partner especially in regard to agricultural products, let us keep our systems parallel. There will be utter confusion and loss of markets if we move to metric ahead of the U.S.A., particularly in agricultural matters.
Let us teach metric in our schools. Let us prepare for it rather than suddenly thrusting it on the people. I hope we can change the direction of the metric system by slowing it down to a stop. In that way there will be some freedom of choice in whether people use it or not.
One lion, member mentioned the case earlier today about a storekeeper in his riding for whom it was going to cost a large sum of money to change his scales. At least five of the storekeepers in the Bow Valley constituency told me during my recent mainstreeting in 42 centres that the change in their stores will bankrupt them. One said his scales alone would cost him $8,000, and another said it would cost him $2,000. He said he could not afford to pay $2,000 for scales just to weigh the few items that required weighing in his store. Let us give some thought to this thing and what it is doing to our country. We do not want to be an island when the world turns metric, but let us not penalize our people, hurt our markets, and destroy the faith of our people by pushing this on them before its time.
We hope to change the direction of legislation, not by bureaucracy or by cabinet orders, but by free debates in this House before passing any laws in respect of which the people should have some input, and before anything is thrust upon them. Some of the cardinal principles of the Progressive Conservative Party are freedom of thought, freedom of choice, and freedom of enterprise.
I believe it was Woodrow Wilson who said:
Liberty has never come from the government. The history of liberty is the history of the limitation of governmental power, not the increase of it.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to be speaking today early in this session of the Thirty-first Parliament. If I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I would like to welcome all our new colleagues sitting in the House of Commons for the first time and wish them well in the exercise of the heavy responsibilities they will have to discharge in the coming months.
Mr. Speaker, in my capacity as the spokesman for my party on tourist matters, I would like first of all to give the House an analysis of the tourist situation in Canada and, second, elaborate briefly on the highlights of a new approach on the tourist issue.
The tourist industry ranks high in the economy of this country. I only have to quote a few figures: $10 billion in tourist revenues which represent 5 per cent of our gross national revenue, with the result that the tourist industry holds fifth place in the economy of this country. Tourism in this country creates 900,000 jobs, 500,000 of which are permanent. The needs for facilities and services created by tourism in Canada require public and private investments of SI.5 billion.

Tourist revenues at all levels of government exceed $4 billion. Also, every dollar spent in the tourist industry has a multiplier factor of $2.40. Finally, the private sector of the tourist industry is made up of 80,000 small competitive businesses, 2,000 travel agencies, 350 carriers and 43,000 restaurants, plus 15,000 hotels. The tourist industry is becoming increasingly important from our social point of view. The Canadian society is becoming increasingly involved in the leisure age, a good part of which is spent on travelling. According to Statistics Canada, the average spending on travelling, tourist activities and recreation accounts for 10 to 15 per cent of the family budget, which is more than substantial.
The tourist industry is also very important in terms of Canadian unity. Travelling Canadians can discover the various areas of this country, discuss with their fellow citizens and get acquainted with the different ethnic and cultural groups that make up the Canadian mosaic. In spite of the figures we just quoted, in spite of the fact, as the hon. member who spoke before me suggested, that the tourist industry is probably the one which is being left the most in the hands and only in the hands of private enterprise, it does not mean that everything is well in the industry. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, the tourism industry in Canada is very sick and it is high time that we find a cure. Let me simply mention that the deficit which was $727 million in 1975 went up to $1.7 billion in 1978 and that, if this trend keeps up, it is estimated that the tourism deficit will reach $10 billion by 1985. This situation is unacceptable and we must react as swiftly as possible. One of the fundamental causes of our deficit is the fact that a large number of Canadians spend their vacation abroad and that we are unable to attract to this country an influx of foreign visitors. For instance, in 1977, 31.8 million Americans came to Canada while 39.4 million Canadians travelled abroad, including 37.9 million to the United States.
Yet, the population of Canada represents only 10 per cent of that of the United States. That same year, more than two million Canadians, of which 31 per cent came from Quebec, spent more than $1 billion in Florida. The devaluation of our dollar in 1978 did nothing to change the situation. Indeed, in spite of a devaluation of 15 per cent compared with American currency and 25 to 50 per cent compared with European currencies, we have kept the same record deficit as in 1977. Moreover, the number of Canadians willing in 1978 to pay 15 to 50 per cent more to travel abroad remained exactly the same as in 1977, which certainly did not help reduce our deficit.
Mr. Speaker, it is important to note that services in the tourist industry cost 20 per cent more in Canada than in the United States. Tourism in Canada is therefore a luxury that 80 per cent of the population cannot afford. The travel price index in Canada rose from 100 in 1971 to 160 in 1976 compared with an increase of 100 to 141 for the same period
October 18, 1979

in the United States. Even though our dollar was devalued by more than 15 per cent, it still cost less to travel to most places outside Canada. For instance, Mr. Speaker, the air fare of $160 from Montreal to Miami is less than the air fare of $192 plus the 8 per cent tax from Montreal to the Magdalen Islands. Yet, the distance is shorter by half. In this regard the government should consider seriously and in depth offering Canadians a greater choice of charter flights to allow lower costs and a greater number of trips within the country.
Let me now go on to another aspect of the tourist industry, namely, the role of travel agencies. We do not object either to the existence or the role of travel agencies since they have their place in tourist planning in Canada, but we would like to underline the matter of the free services offered by these agencies. Even though they claim that their services are free, it is certainly false since the 2,000 Canadian travel agents in 1977 raked in $2 billion of which only 20 per cent remained in Canada. The companies involved in tourism pay commissions of 7 to 15 per cent to travel agencies, 7 to 8 per cent on airplane tickets, 10 to 12 per cent on organized trips, 10 per cent on charter flights, 10 to 15 per cent on car rentals and 8 to 10 per cent on hotel costs.
Travellers cannot therefore save on those commissions by purchasing directly from companies. Those who drive their own cars and arrive directly at the hotel indirectly pay to hotelkeepers commissions to agents they did not use. That should be corrected. We would consider reducing those companies' rates by the amount paid as commissions to travel agencies, and force the latter to charge their commissions directly to their clients.
Quite apart from that, we regret that travel agencies do not advertise enough to convince people to travel in Canada. Go to any agency, you will find that more than 80 per cent of packages offered for sale have foreign destinations. We also feel on this side of the House that the issue of wages and salaries in the tourist industry is of the outmost importance. It is vital that a wage policy be developed as soon as possible for the tourist industry. Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to deal briefly with another aspect of a more geographic nature, namely, our climate. Many people argue that our Canadian climate and especially our Canadian winter is not good for tourism. We believe, Mr. Speaker, it is high time we take a more positive approach.
We are fortunate in having four seasons quite distinct, each with its charms and beauty. This is an asset of which we should take advantage of. To those who decry winter, I would say that it lends itself to a variety of inside and outside activities. We never exploited our winter season enough to promote tourism. I am sure that with well designed publicity campaigns we could attract large number of tourists from the warmer countries, to whom snow and winter are novelties. The same advertisements could also make Canadians aware of the beauties and opportunities of our Canadian winter.
The Address-Mr. Loiselle
Mr. Speaker, I have referred to advertising. Over the last few years, tourist publicity in every form has increased considerably. We should examine seriously the quality of that publicity. Obviously, our publicity does not really attempt to put the accent on the particular attractions of Canada. In fact, 80 to 90 per cent of the tourist publicity in Canadian mass media by airlines and travel agencies encourages Canadians to visit foreign countries and particularly the United States. It is true that it is much more profitable for a travel agency to sell a complete package to Miami than a return flight to Vancouver. We can realize the seriousness of the situation every day in our newspapers, periodicals and magazines.
The publicity budget of the Canadian Office of Tourism for 1979-80 is roughly $10 million. Of that amount, $5.9 million is for the United States, $2.6 million for the rest of the world and only $1.5 million for Canada. We complain about our deficit and the small number of Canadians who are visiting our country. It is not with only 15 per cent of our publicity budget spent in Canada that we shall convince Canadians to visit their own country. Mr. Speaker, we simply must increase the amounts spent on publicity in Canada. First we should promote tourism in our country rather than abroad.
The government expressed its concern about government spending. We suggest that it should study carefully the publicity budget of the Canadian Office of Tourism and particularly the $5.9 million spent for the United States to check if the return on those spendings justify the cost and, if not, to allocate those amounts to publicity in Canada.
To illustrate the seriousness of the whole situation, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote some brief statistics concerning some periodicals, for instance Evasion. .This publication that calls itself the only great French monthly periodical about travel, holidays and recreation in Canada has been published since November, 1975. In 27 issues which appeared since that date until October, 1978, this periodical published articles about Canada in 12 editions, about Quebec in 19 and about Florida in 25. Those figures do not need any comment and are unacceptable. Furthermore, Canada is certainly one of the countries which publish the largest number of tourist information. But that avalanche of publications with a profusion of superlatives does not allow a foreigner any more than a Canadian to prepare his travel in advance. Often it does not even encourage him to do it. Canada is very little known as our pamphlets and folders are like very short range rifles, they do not cross the Canadian borders or even the provincial borders.
Still, Canada does offer many tourist attractions capable of motivating a transatlantic trip, but they are not always publicized adequately, in that those which we praise most here are not necessarily those that are the most eagerly sought after by people outside North America. Our tourist concepts do not necessarily correspond with the tastes of the Spanish or the Germans. The European, for instance, generally attaches much greater importance to history, art and folklore. pleases him more than do the great American tourist attractions. Old Montreal and Mount Royal would therefore be far more appreciated than the buildings of Place Ville-Marie.
Mr. Speaker, I am not exaggerating when I say that here, in Canada, there is no truly organized tourist industry. For years now, governments, federal and provincial, private enterprise, have been going ahead with their promotions, according to their own whims and small concerns. There is no real tourist policy in Canada. There is a free-for-all. Mr. Speaker, that situation cannot last any longer. We must plan, even now, our tourist development for the 1980s. That is a priority we must set for ourselves.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to elaborate on a few suggestions 1 discussed with a citizen whom I have learned to admire greatly because of his thorough knowledge of tourism. 1 am speaking here of a citizen who really thinks in terms of the interest of his country, namely, Mr. Jean-Marie Guay of Gatineau. I was also deeply interested in the proposal of the Minister of Tourism with regard to developing an over-all strategy for tourism in Canada. Mr. Speaker, we too feel that our tourist deficit is of prime concern. In that regard, with the co-operation of Mr. Guay, I looked into certain measures designed to reduce our deficit, and as an example we took the case of Quebec.
Statistics indicate that 52 per cent of Quebeckers do not travel. If half of these 52 per cent of Quebeckers had spent $180 travelling in 1976, that is the average spent by those Quebeckers who do travel, this average of $365, Quebec's $200 million deficit would have been replaced by a $50 million surplus. If the duration of the trips made by Quebeckers in Quebec had been extended by 10 per cent, $70 million could have been recovered from the 1976 deficit. If the number of Quebeckers travelling outside Quebec had been reduced from 24 to 20 per cent, and if these Quebeckers had spent in Quebec half of the average of $365, the deficit could have been reduced by $45 million. A 30 per cent increase in non-American foreign tourists would have brought in an additional $30 million. A 15 per cent increase in Canadian tourists from other provinces would have brought in $15 million in additional revenues. A 10 per cent increase in American tourists would bring $15 million more.
Mr. Speaker, these measures could be applied to Canada as a whole without much difficulty. Contrary to what occurs in other areas, there is probably in Canada and elsewhere in the world no organization, eitheir public or private, which is involved in serious research in tourist leisure and the implementation of its findings. Many people have some experience in the tourism industry, but as far as I know there is no real graduate in that field. First of all, Mr. Speaker, it seems important to me to consider the creation of an independent tourism research and development institute. This institute

would be financed by both public funds and private funds coming from associations involved in tourist matters. Once set up, the institute would, as a first step, evaluate the Canadian tourist product as well as current and potential, customers for that product.
The Canadian tourist product is more than just natural beauties or historic sites. A full evaluation of the tourist product would also look at the whole service sector-the carriers, hotels, restaurants and tourist circuits. That step seems to me of prime importance. How could one expect, Mr. Speaker, to develop any tourist strategy if one has not beforehand made an inventory of what are the country's tourist attractions, development potential, and customers to develop it?
The institute being an independent agency, its evaluation of the product would be most objective since it would not have to yield to parochial interests. So the end result of this evaluation would take into account only those tourist attractions and services which are most worth while and eliminate a great many others which have very little interest.
There is no intention on my part to favour one region at the expense of another but one must understand that not everything is worth seeing in Canada and that we must first develop what is most profitable. The evaluation of our tourist product would enable us to establish uniform classification criteria for the services available. For instance, the traveller would know that a three-maple-leaf hotel or restaurant has the same meaning in Vancouver as it does in St. John's, Newfoundland, which would quite often spare him very unpleasant surprises and would largely contribute to the elimination of a great many exploiters who make a living out of the false representation of the services rendered.
The identification of the clientele would allow for better planning of our tourist development in accordance with the varying tastes of travellers. It is as important to provide the culture minded type of visitor with a product that will capture his interest as it is in the case of the sports fan or the travelling gourmet. The proposed institute could play a leading role in the preparation of training programs for tourist agents who, once defined, could become precious instruments for the provincial departments of education. The institute could also raise the interest of young people for tourism. Students and youngsters are the future of our country. The institute could develop certain instruments such as, for instance, tourist educational games which could be integrated as complements to the social sciences courses provided in the schools. The institute could also carry out marketing studies in the field of tourism and try to improve on the Canadian product.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that this institute should have an independent status. This must not be construed as a refusal to co-operate with the various levels of government and private enterprise engaged in the development of tourism. The institute could also make governments and the private sector

involved in tourism benefit from the results of its research by recommending initiatives to be taken in the area of tourist infrastructure and the development of their tourist strategy. The creation of a tourist research and development institute would not have to compete with government and private agents already working in this area. It would be an additional tool to promote tourism in Canada.
We also consider, Mr. Speaker, that the work already being done by the various levels of government must continue. We recognize that the federal government has a major role to play in the promotion of tourism in Canada. It should be involved in the establishment of tourism development policies, in publicity and also in the area of tax incentives provided to private business in the tourism sector. We urge the government to inform us as soon as possible of its response to the Powell report recommendations concerning taxation in the tourist sector.
We must also reconsider the approach and the objectives of the federal government when negotiating federal-provincial agreements concerning the tourist industry, to avoid certain waste of public money, and, to be very clear, to avoid repeating the exercise experienced in Quebec where we have spent over $75 million sprinkling grants all across the province instead of developing one, two or three regions, instead of concentrating our efforts in these regions to attract specific customers.
We must also-and a Progressive Conservative government,
1 hope, should convince banks-facilitate the access of the private sector to risk capital, because the tourist industry needs large investments which are practically unobtainable because of the unreliability of this supply in public funds.
Also, Mr. Speaker, we will have to review the functions of national parks within a global tourist strategy in Canada. Allow me now to sum up our position. As I have said, our tourist industry is in bad shape and we will have to find a remedy as soon as possible. We believe that the Canadian tourist industry must be included in a large industrial strategy so that it could enjoy the same advantages that other industries already have.
We think that the development of a national tourist strategy must be made in direct consultation with all levels of government and private entreprises operating in that field. In this regard, we hope that the next federal-provincial conference of tourism ministers which will take place later this month will result in better planning and co-ordination of policies and investment.
We also believe that the creation of a tourism research and development institute is a very important move for the development of tourism in Canada. Mr. Speaker, tourism and its development are important resources for all Canadians. The time has come now to develop those resources not only for us but specially for future generations.

The Address-Mr. Gass

1 wish to begin by adding my sincere congratulations to the many already expressed to you, Mr. Speaker and to the Deputy Speaker on your reappointments. May you continue to preside over the affairs of the House in the same efficient and non-partisan manner, and with the same degree of fairness you demonstrated in the previous Parliament.
Before going any further I would like to comment on the speech made by the hon. member on the other side. I am glad to know the party opposite is finally showing interest in tourism, which is something it neglected to do over the last 11 years. We support most of what the hon. gentleman has just said.
As well, I congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald). I should especially like to express my delight with the speech given by my friend and fellow islander, the hon. member for Cardigan, as his rural constituency is not unlike the one which I have been chosen to represent. I am indeed honoured to be here in the House of Commons delivering my maiden speech. I hope I can serve the constituents of Malpeque as well as they were served for 25 years by my PC predecessor and now premier of Prince Edward Island, the Hon. Angus MacLean.
Hear, hear!

May I also express my gratitude to the good people of Malpeque for placing me here and assure my constituents that it is my intention to serve them to the best of my ability, whether 1 am here in Ottawa or at home in my riding.
It could be said that the constituency of Malpeque which I represent is the incarnation of what everyone who is not an islander believes Prince Edward Island to be. The Micmac Indians knew Prince Edward Island as Abegweit, meaning cradled on the waves, and the island has often been referred to as the million acre farm, or Canada's garden province.
We in Malpeque are blessed with fertile rolling farmland, bountiful waters, and beautiful sandy beaches. Thus agriculture, fisheries, and tourism are the three major industries that keep the majority of the people of Malpeque happy, healthy, and employed. The three industries are like a three-legged stool, each leg or industry supporting and complementing the other two.
Every year the land produces an abundance of potatoes, a quality potato which is shipped throughout the world and for which Prince Edward Island has become famous. But we do not grow only potatoes. The spud may be king, but there are other crops and produce such as grain, dairy cattle, beef cattle, and hogs, that are of significant importance to the Malpeque farmers. Prince Edward Island in known as the Kentucky of Canada because of the quality harness racing and the stand-ardbred horses that are raised on the island. However, no

October 18, 1979
The Address-Mr. Gass
matter what the product, we on Prince Edward Island are proud of what we produce, and equally proud of the hard working people who produce it.
Much of the same thing could be said of the fisheries industry in Malpeque as has been said of the agricultural industry. Malpeque is well known for its lobster and its lobster suppers, its oysters, and for its giant biue fin tuna.
M-m-m-m-m-m-m!

During the often too short fishing seasons, men and women work long and hard to bring in the products of the sea for which Prince Edward Island is famous. It was especially encouraging for me to see that the future development of our fisheries resources was considered in the Speech from the Throne. Such development is necessary if those who live off the sea are to continue to live as they have, and to further improve their lot. Canada needs its fisheries industry, and only through expansion and improvement of the industry will our country be able to maintain its position as one of the major fishing and fish exporting nations of the world.
I have already had occasion to mention how proud we are in Prince Edward Island of our products which possess such high quality. This quality has been the result of a collective effort on the part of the people, the result of good, honest, hard work. For the people who live from the land and the sea, work is not a four-letter word. They are proud of what they do and proud of the effort they put into doing it. I am sorry to say that the general attitude toward work has changed over the past half century as science and technology became more advanced. At one time work was a source of pride and joy for all men and women. It is our duty not only to stimulate the economy by providing more jobs, but we must also seek the means to create a greater desire in the populace to be employed.
Work is not a burden to be endured or avoided but should be looked on as a source of pride, a sense of accomplishment and achievement for a job well done. As a member of the PC caucus committee on tourism, one of the highlights of the Speech from the Throne for me was the fact that mention was made of the tourism industry, and I quote: "In co-operation with the provinces and industry, a national tourism strategy will be developed."
In Prince Edward Island tourism, along with agriculture and fisheries, is one of the three major industries and sources of revenue and one of the fastest growing industries on the island. As I have already had occasion to note, we in the constituency of Malpeque are blessed with beautiful, sandy beaches. Malpeque is the home of Prince Edward Island's only national park, which stretches for approximately 21 miles along the island's north shore and which is perhaps Prince Edward Island's most famous landmark and tourist haven. My riding is also recognized worldwide as the home of Anne of Green Gables, the fictitious little island girl made famous by island born authoress, Lucy Maude Montgomery. Lucy Maude, well known for her "Anne" stories, has also immortalized the beauty of and her love for the island, in her poetry. "The Island Hymn," written by Miss Montgomery, expresses her

feelings as well as those of many islanders. With Your Honour's permission, I will quote it:
Fair island of the sea,
We raise our song to thee,
The bright and blest;
Loyally now we stand As brothers, hand in hand,
And sing God save the land We love the best.
Upon our princely isle May kindest fortune smile In coming years;
Peace and prosperity In all her borders be.
From every evil free, and weakling fears.
Prince Edward Isle, to thee Our hearts shall faithful be.
Where'er we dwell;
Forever may we stand As brothers, hand in hand,
And sing God save the land We love so well.
People who "come in from away" to Prince Edward Island are not disappointed, for islanders put their heart and soul into making their province a place where visitors can relax and enjoy themselves, and learn what good, simple living is all about. During the summer months our tourism industry not only employs thousands of our students, but provides an income for many families, one which they live on year round. Thus tourism is of the utmost importance to Malpeque, Prince Edward Island, and Canada as a whole.
The fact is that tourism in Canada is an $11 billion business accounting for 5 per cent of the gross national product, and employing one person in every ten. Eighty per cent of the tourist businesses are classified as small business. For too many years this important sector of the economy was virtually overlooked by previous administrations, and this must be changed. The government must also endeavour to develop a program of awareness for the public of Canada. Canadians all across the country should be made aware of the importance of the tourist industry to the economy and to the country. If tourism is to succeed and flourish as a major industry in Canada, it is of the greatest importance that the Canadian people understand its great and valued impact on the country.
Transportation is another major concern of mine, Mr. Speaker, for in order to serve our basic industries in Prince Edward Island we need adequate transportation systems; better ferries, better roads, and improved rail and air services to and on the island. In order for our agriculture and fisheries industries to remain viable, an upgrading of the systems that transport their products to markets must take place. Such upgrading in reference to Prince Edward Island would include better roads, better port facilities, and improved ferry and rail service, and an overhaul of air service. The tourism industry also depends heavily on how efficiently the transportation
October 18, 1979

system to and on Prince Edward Island is operating. We are, however, in the process of acquiring new airport facilities, a step in the right direction, I might add. What improvements that are being made to our transportation systems to and on Prince Edward Island are slow in coming, and few and far between. 1 hope that in the near future attention will be given to this matter of such great importance to Prince Edward Island and its industries.
As a member concerned about the plight of the farmer, the fisherman, and the small businessman of my constituency, it upsets me to see interest rates continuously increasing. Such increases are a disincentive to the expansion of small business and industry and one must sympathize with a person who is already in business and who has a loan with a floating interest rate-always up, it seems. This government will have to do everything within its power to bring interest rates down to a reasonable level.
I have spent the last few moments speaking of matters and issues which are of major concern to Malpeque and Prince Edward Island. Now I would like to continue for just a few moments addressing you on a subject which has always been and always will be of the utmost importance to me, that is, the role of the youth in Malpeque, in Prince Edward Island, and in Canada. The youth of this country are of special interest to me. 1 have a very deep and abiding concern for our young people. They have so much to contribute; it is a shame to see a great deal of this energy and potential going to waste. What do you tell a youngster about the kind of job he can expect to have when he leaves school, Mr. Speaker? It saddens me to see the disillusionment of our young people because they are not able to find meaningful work.
Bitterness and frustration are evident among many of our young Canadians who finish school and are unable to find jobs. We spend millions of dollars educating our youth and the only opportunity many of them get to utilize their skills is in completing UIC forms. It is time we re-arranged our priorities. We must start spending more assisting private enterprise and small business, thus creating an environment where more jobs are available.
It pleased me to see that the Speech from the Throne proposed the passing of legislation which would encourage small business and private enterprise, as well as the creation of a youth employment secretariat. It is important that the youth of Canada have faith in the political and parliamentary process of our country. It is important we continue to endeavour to provide a favourable climate in which our youth can live and work, for only then will we be able to keep our young people at home, only then will we be able to participate in the continuing development of Canada. In the past, Prince Edward Island has had problems keeping its youth at home after they finish their formal schooling. In the words of the Speech from the Throne we need to assist all individual Canadians, but especially our youth, in "building a stake in our country .
The Address-Mr. Gass
I should like to make mention of an issue which concerns the whole of the Canadian populace, in particular the youth. Because of my long involvement with young people and my deep and abiding concern for their welfare, I feel it is incumbent on governments, both federal and provincial, to establish an educational program advising Canadians on the more recent information about marijuana and other drugs and their adverse effects. I feel the lack of education is the crux of the whole drug problem, and that such an educational program, once established, will go a long way in helping our young people to understand the problems that can arise from the adverse usage of drugs.
I should like to go on for just a moment to deal with another matter which, in an indirect fashion, concerns young Canadians. If we are to expect our youth to have faith in our country's political and parliamentary process, if we are to expect our young people to have respect for those in positions such as we hold as members of Parliament, we are, first of all, going to have to show a little more respect for each other as we sit here in the House of Commons debating and making decisions on matters that concern our country.
It appalls me, Mr. Speaker, to witness the lack of respect that is present as individual members address the House. It may be difficult for some members to refrain from showing ignorance and lack of manners, but I do wish they would begin to show some politeness. Now that these sessions are being broadcast across the country for all to see, Canadians are able to view what they could only read about before-the thumping and pounding, the catcalls and the rude remarks. Is this how we endeavour to see that our youth respect the institutions we represent? As this first session of the Thirty-first Parliament continues I sincerely hope many of you will take a good, long look at yourselves and your actions here in the House, not only for the sake of the youth in the country but for your own sakes as well.
As many before me have stated, ours is a new Parliament facing an enormous challenge. Let us endeavour to live up to the expectations that Canadians have for us. And, Mr. Speaker, may we not disappoint them.
Mr. Speaker, I seek the indulgence of the House as I have only three or four minutes left. Could I call it ten o'clock and make my speech tomorrow afternoon?

NORTHERN AFFAIRS-PROVINCIAL STATUS FOR THE YUKON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before coming to the subject, 1 should like to congratulate you on your appointment as Deputy Speaker of the House. As a neighbour in the constituency of Chateauguay, 1 can tell you that it is an honour for the whole area of the valley of Chateauguay.

Last week, Mr. Speaker, 1 alleged in a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) that the effect of recent instructions issued by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Epp), specifically the removal of the commissioner of the executive committee in the Yukon, is to grant de facto provincial status to that territory without the consent either of Parliament or of the Yukon electorate, not to mention the other provinces in confederation. Surely this contention is not in any doubt.
1 quote from the letter of instruction which was issued to the commissioner by the minister, which led to her resignation: the commissioner was instructed to request the territorial government leader that he constitute and appoint a body known as the cabinet to replace the executive committee. She was then told in that same letter, "You will not be a member of the cabinet or of the executive committee and will not participate on a day to day basis in the affairs of the cabinet." Then, to make the meaning absolutely clear, the commissioner was informed that she had to remove herself physically from the legislative building. If there is any doubt anywhere that the intention of the minister was to create de facto provincehood by his instruction I need only refer to the authorization contained in the minister's press release-I presume it was also included in the letter-to the effect that the chairman of the executive council could call himself premier.
When I asked the Prime Minister the question last week he replied that he was surprised that the spokesman for our party was not enthusiastic about an extension of democracy in our country. Let us just consider the question of responsible government. Does the Yukon have it now? What measure of responsible government does it have? Until this last event the commissioner had been instructed by the previous government, to accept the advice of the majority leader as to the number of members ol the executive, and following the last territorial election the commissioner was also instructed to accept the advice of the majority leader on the appointment of elected members to the executive committee. In addition, this executive committee had control over matters of local importance

and matters of concern to provincial governments such as health, roads, education, and the administration of justice.
These matters were all being looked after by this executive committee long before this recent initiative of the minister. Although he may have obtained some advice from his advisers, and they in turn may have received some advice from the Department of Justice, I certainly have very serious doubts as to the legality of at least part of what the minister has initiated in this instance.
The commissioner resigned. The commissioner did not resign in a tiff. She was not a bureaucrat who was insulted by these actions of the minister. If any white has a right to call herself a native Yukoner, she has. Her roots go back two or three generations in the Yukon. Without question she was and is one of the most esteemed personages in the north.
At the time of her selection last January she was the unanimous choice of all Yukoners. Suddenly in October she had to resign, and she resigned because she felt it her duty to resign, presumably in the interests of the Yukon and Yukoners.
It seems to me that the minister has placed himself in an unfortunate situation. 1 was happy to see him elevated to minister. I felt he was sympathetic toward native people. I felt he was open and frank and would be an excellent minister. He has been, to use the phrase of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander), bamboozled here by his colleague from Yukon, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Nielsen), who is a very astute individual and who realized perhaps-this may be one of the reasons, at least-that the Drury report will be forthcoming within the next few weeks. Certainly if any of Mr. Drury's statements so far find their way into his report, we can expect some recommendations about local government in the Northwest Territories.
The report does not address itself to the Yukon, but presumably there is some fear in some quarters that there may be some interesting stuff in that Drury report, and people of the Yukon may perhaps be interested in making use of some of that material. Those who are not interested in seeing that happen want, in effect, to pre-empt that danger. In fact by pre-empting that danger they are pre-judging the referendum the Yukon has been promised on the whole question of provincial status. They are pre-judging the electorate and, in effect, pre-empting their right to decide in one way or another.
.. T,he referendum will have to deal not just with a "yes" and a "no" question, but it appears it will not even reach that point if the minister, taking advice from his colleague in the cabinet, the Minister of Public Works, has his way. The die will have been cast, and that is what has happened in this situation. We now have de facto provincial status in the Yukon without reference to Parliament, without reference to the electorate of the Yukon, and without reference, as the Prime Minister has promised, to the premiers of the provinces.
There are a number of questions we can ask. The financial implications for Yukoners themselves are serious. The Yukon
October 18, 1979

is presently receiving from the federal government about $23 million a year for operating expenses, another $15 million for capital expenses, plus the $13 million or so which is being raised by its taxpayers and which, presumably, in the next year or so will be the subject of an income tax system within the Yukon itself.
I would like to terminate by requesting the minister to reconsider his position to allow, first, a consideration of this change by a parliamentary committee and, second, to reconsider the change in the commissioner's role. It is certainly not a change which is in the interest of the people of the Yukon or of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his question. I know he is sincere about his views, but I must say to him that my views are diametrically opposed to his, which have been stated by the former government, that colonial status must remain north of 60. That is a position that this government does not accept.
The point should be mentioned also that he talks about the fact of provincial status. I do not know what the fact of provincial status is because we have never had that in our Canadian experience, but I want to say to him, first, that the Yukon does not have control over land; second, it does not have control over resources; third, it does not have control over fiscal responsibility. In fact I said in the letter of instructions to the former commissioner that the budget was to be looked at by the elected people and only then submitted to her and passed on to Ottawa. So when the hon. member speaks about provincial status, whatever definition he might have, it does not square with the facts.
What the government has done through the letter of instructions to the commissioner of the Yukon has been to provide the Yukon with responsible government as far as the Yukon Act allows. The Yukon Act provides that the commissioner receive instructions from time to time from the minister with respect to the ways in which the government of the day wishes the commissioner to carry out his or her duties. In fact the former minister said very similar things, and I quote from his letter of instructions. It reads;
In response to territorial requests for further transfers of delegation of responsibilities to the Yukon, the federal government wishes to be as forthcoming and as flexible as possible. Our aim is to achieve full, responsible government in the Yukon while ensuring that the interest and participation of the Yukon Indians are fully guaranteed.
They are almost exactly the same words as I used in my own letter, which reads:
It is clear to me that prior to the introduction of legislative changes in the Yukon Act it will be necessary for me to ensure that measures are developed which will protect the interests of native people in the Yukon and ensure their full and effective participation in government.
On the matter of consultation, I was in the Yukon, I met with the Yukon territorial government and I met with the Council of Yukon Indians while I was there. In fact on Friday,
