Mr. Speaker,
I should like to join with my colleague in congratulating Your Honour on your elevation to the role of Deputy Speaker. I know the very fine job Your Honour has done in the past. I am pleased that the House is in such good hands.
On Tuesday I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) a question about a Mexican oil trade deal that we were in the process of negotiating before we slipped from power.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You mean fell.

Only slipped slightly. In January our minister met with his counterpart in Mexico, along with officials from Petro-Canada and Pemex, and eventually met with the President of Mexico, Senor Fopez Portillo. They agreed to a long term, ten-year oil deal involving something in the order of $5 billion to $6 billion worth of Mexican oil for Canadian goods and services in roughly the same amount. This deal was then put on paper and initialed by our minister and the Mexican ambassador on May 4 or 5, with the expectation that the President of Mexico would come to Canada in September and
390

October 18, 1979
Adjournment Debate
that there would be a proper signing of this document. After that there would be some negotiations between Petro-Canada and Pemex to bring the deal into fruition. It was hoped that by this winter we would have 10,000 barrels of oil a day coming to the east coast from Mexico.
I asked the Prime Minister why the visit of the President of Mexico had been postponed, whether indeed it had been postponed, or whether indeed the deal actually had fallen through. The Prime Minister assured me that the trip had to be postponed, but he said nothing about whether the deal had or had nor fallen through. He indicated that the Mexican president would visit Canada in May of 1980. There is no question that there has been a postponement, otherwise some kind of an arrangement could have been made for an earlier signature. I am not sure a signature is possible come next spring.
I should like to question what probably has gone wrong. I think there has been a lack of understanding on the part of this government of the history of Mexico, how Mexicans feel about oil, who produces and sells their oil and to whom they sell. We must not forget that the Mexicans went through a revolution in early 1920s to shake off American oil interests. It was made plain to all and sundry that the Mexicans did not want to deal with the multinationals, the Seven Sisters. They wanted to deal state to state. I think there is also a parallel with Venezuela where the Venezuelans decided not to go through with the deal involving 100,000 barrels per day to Petro-Canada through their oil company PetroVen, because during the election there were expectations that the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) might become Prime Minister and that his government would break up PetroCan and the deal would not go through. I think most of these countries are very wary of dealing with a government which does not put any faith in a national oil company.
There is another problem which I think may have occurred, and that is the problem of dealing with the government of Japan and the Japanese petroleum exploration company that also made some overtures to Mexico. It looks to me like they have outsmarted us. I cannot prove at this particular point that we have lost $5 billion or $6 billion worth of business, but I am certain there has been a postponement. There may be a shortfall this winter and we will need additional amounts.
I am very concerned that this government does not believe it wise to keep the national oil company in there in order that it may make this kind of deal. I am concerned that the government does not feel the national oil company should be made stronger and stronger for this purpose. I am afraid that the Mexicans and Venezuelans will look very askance at the kind of establishment we are going to set up after we give away the assets. I think they will have some doubts about this agency that is to be created with a lot of debts and not too much expertise, the best parts having gone. If this happens, I believe we will actually lose this deal which could mean 100,000

man-years of work for Canadians if the trade aspects are followed through.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Jarvis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the question put and the statements made by the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae), may I first point out that I had always understood, certainly when I went to school, that the revolution in Mexico in the 1920s, which included some of the activities of Pancho Villa, was a fight over the question of poverty and the oppression of the people by a dictatorship. I did not realize that they were fighting oil companies at that time. If my friend's speculations are as sound as his history, then there is very little to be said in respect of his speculations.
I would, however, respectfully point out to the hon. member that an Energy Co-operation Agreement was initialled by the Canadian and Mexican governments on May 4, 1979. Article
11	of the agreement looks forward to a minimum delivery of 10,000 barrels a day of crude oil commencing in 1979 or 1980. Those were the terms of that original memorandum of agreement. Deliveries of larger volumes will follow over the ensuing
12	months.
A separate Industrial Co-operation Agreement was initialled at the same time, and there is no barter connection between the supply of Mexican oil as referred to in the Energy Co-operation Agreement or in the memorandun or the Industrial Co-operation Agreement which was signed at the same time.
At the same time as the Energy Co-operation Agreement was being negotiated, discussions were taking place with Mexican officials about the details of future supply of oil to Canada. A commitment was received from Pemex, the Mexican national oil company, for deliveries of small quantities to begin in the second half of 1980 to the extent that production will permit once their existing commitments are met. That does not include any commitment to the Japanese, so there is no foundation to the speculation the hon. member posed in that regard. Deliveries to Canada are to be increased beyond that level in accordance with the availability of their supplies.
Contacts have been maintained with the Mexican government and with Pemex since the agreement was initialled. A Canadian delegation headed by the assistant deputy minister for energy visited Mexico City in September. It discussed Mexican production forecasts for 1980, which will determine the date when supplies will commence. A second visit is to be made in December at the Mexicans' suggestion, when further information as to future deliveries will be made available. That hardly suggests that the deal is at an end or is not going forward, particularly when at the Mexican suggestion we are attending that meeting to fix the times when deliveries commence. I trust that satisfies the questions and statements put by the hon. member.
October 18, 1979

subtopic: ENERGY-SUPPLY OF GASOLINE AND HEATING OIL THIS WINTER
ENERGY-SUPPLY OF GASOLINE AND HEATING OIL THIS WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday I raised with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) the problem of the supply of fuel, oil and gasoline being down in Ontario. Indeed, we have learned that the reserves of home heating oil are down over 18 per cent from the same period last year, and gasoline supply by some 20 per cent. If members will recall, last year in Ontario the supply situation was very tight. Indeed, we have learned that British Petroleum has been closing its gas stations on Sundays and that Shell has been reducing the hours of operation of its gas stations as well, all of which, of course, indicates that there is a serious supply problem facing us in the months ahead.
What is more worrisome is that the oil companies in many cases have not bid on traditional fuel oil contracts for large users such as school boards. Indeed, in the area from which I come, and in nearby Algoma, a number of school boards have not been receiving the traditional bids from the oil companies to supply them with fuel, nor have they been offering the traditional discounts to large users. When I raised this matter in the House on Monday, I pointed out to the minister that we have a very fragile situation. In fact, those were the words he used. I wanted from him some kind of assurance that we would be able to make it through the winter without any problems.
I am still not satisfied that we will be able to do so. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence) has admitted that he is powerless to do anything with the oil companies which are refusing to make their normal bids. I think that that is a sad statement, considering the power which the federal government has at its disposal. It really puts us again at the mercy of the private oil companies, the majority of which are foreign-controlled, at a time when we are about to, if we believe this government, disband Petro-Canada.
It seems to me that the situation will only get worse. The other thing that I pointed out to the minister is that the department of consumer affairs for the past six years has been investigating these oil companies on suspicion that they have been manipulating supply and price. I understand that the department will soon bring forward a report and that there is a likelihood that criminal charges will be laid. All of this makes me very suspicious about why we are facing shortages this winter, or potential shortages.
The oil companies tell us that there have been refinery breakdowns and this accounts for the lower supplies. We also know that gasoline demand was up over the summer and that many of the refineries were not producing home heating oil but converting to gasoline production instead. But the mere fact that we have this ongoing investigation into the supply practices in the oil companies makes me wonder if those are the real reasons, and to that end I asked the minister in the House whether or not he would make public the reports of the National Energy Board as to the supply situation because we,
Adjournment Debate
as members of Parliament, and the public generally, do not have access to these reports.
I think it is important that we be able to determine to our own satisfaction what the reasons for this downturn in supplies are. The minister, I think, misunderstood me when I asked that question because he thought I was referring to the investigation by the combines branch of the consumer affairs department. What I wanted to know was whether or not he would make those National Energy Board fuel reports public.
The other point was that the minister, by agreeing that the supply situation was very fragile, made me worry in the sense that all he was saying was that they were monitoring the situation and he was hopeful that we would make it through the winter without any problem. I categorize that statement as a rather bland assurance to the consumers in Ontario. What I wanted to know from the minister was what kind of contingency plans the government has in place in the sad event that we do come up with shortages over the cold months.
Members know that in the spring, before the election, we passed the Energy Supplies Emergency Act which the Conservatives opposed, unfortunately. It gives the federal government some rather sweeping powers to allocate supply to regions that experience shortages and, if it needs to, to implement rationing.
From statements made by the minister in this House and the fact that members of the energy supply allocation board have not yet been appointed, I do not think the government has any contingency plans in place to enable it to react quickly to a shortage if it occurs. The second question I would like answered tonight is this: does the government have any plans in place to meet a fuel oil shortage so that consumers, especially in the more remote parts of the province, will not experience shortages and cold homes over the winter months?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Jarvis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-SUPPLY OF GASOLINE AND HEATING OIL THIS WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the question put by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), may I say that all of us on the government side join with him in expressing concern over a growing world problem, namely, the limited supply of a non-renewable resource which the world as a whole is using beyond its capacity, and beyond reasonable expectations for that resource to last.
One of the prime objectives of this government will be to urge and to lead all Canadians to conserve this limited resource, and to use the resource in a more meaningful and proper manner.
With respect to the questions put, I would advise the hon. member that the government has undertaken several measures to ensure adequate supplies of gasoline and heating oil for this winter. First, they include curtailing crude oil exports to keep pipeline-fed Canadian refineries fully supplied-and I am sure that the hon. member is aware of the dramatic cutbacks in the export of crude oil; second, facilitating the exchange of western Canadian oil for additional eastern seaboard imports,

October 18, 1979
Adjournment Debate
which will increase supply in an area dependent upon oil for much of its energy.
The oil industry is programming a very high rate of delivery of refinery raw material from domestic and overseas sources in the fourth quarter and a commensurately large product market. If these programs can be achieved, then inventories of middle distillates for diesel and heating oil should be close to desirable levels by the year end.
A national outlook for the first quarter of 1980 is that programmed supply should be adequate to meet forecasted product demands, given normal weather conditions, with an acceptable closing inventory level.
Quebec and Ontario seem to be the principal regional trouble spots. The brunt of the oil product supply stringency has been felt in central Canada at the reseller level. Companies affected include medium-sized resellers, who sell both at retail
and wholesale levels, and retail sellers of gasoline and heating oils.
Officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the National Energy Board are keeping in close touch with these resellers, seeking by all possible means to create the conditions for them to get product supply. As well, officials are in frequent contact with refiners having crude oil or products supply difficulties. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has formally urged refiners to treat the resellers fairly. Officials are keeping in close touch with industry and the provinces. The current reading on the situation is "tight but manageable". We have to learn to be a conserving society.
I trust that answers the hon. member's question, Mr. Speaker.
